harder.updated_question: 5.1	Definition and elements of social systems
harder.verification_criterion: The answer defines what a social system is and identifies multiple distinct elements or components that constitute social systems.

attempts.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed definition of social systems and their core elements, synthesized across classical sociological theory, general systems theory, and contemporary systems-of-practice perspectives.

Definition and scope
- A social system is a purposive whole formed by a set of interrelated social elements—people, roles, institutions, meanings, and actions—whose reciprocal relations produce emergent properties that cannot be reduced to any single element alone. <cite id="4db2cf77-1">A system is a whole of elements or parts that are related to one another in a unit; when applied to society, a social system is a whole of social elements that are related and influence each other</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">A social system is not an empirically given concrete reality but a theoretical model that defines certain relations between components of action; from the system’s perspective, orientation and action are expressed in position and role and in patterns of expectations that determine appropriate behavior</cite>.
- Social systems are open, boundary-delineated organizations of interacting parts coupled to environments from which they take inputs and to which they export outputs via flows of matter, energy, information, and feedback. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">A system is a complex network of interacting elements that continuously interact with their environments, transform and evolve, and course-correct based on feedback; social systems include patterns and networks of individuals in groups and structures that carry out diverse functions</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">A system is a coherent entity with discernible boundaries distinguishing internal and external elements and identifying input–output relationships</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">Explicitly defining system boundaries and internal networks of interdependencies is crucial; systems can be composed of subsystems (e.g., households, firms, government), with identified hazards, exposed elements, governance/institutions, and desired outcomes</cite>.
- As complex adaptive and relational entities, social systems are often analyzed as sets of interdependent components that self-organize and reproduce through interactions, creating and maintaining system distinctions (self/other, inside/outside). <cite id="4db2cf77-0">In complex adaptive systems, “components” and “interactions” are operative; social systems exhibiting fission–fusion dynamics can be framed by defining components and their interactions</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">A social system emerges when communication develops from communicative acts; society is relational without including human individuals as elements of the system itself, emphasizing that meaningful utterances received by others and conveying meaningful information are necessary for communication</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Social systems are characterized by structural and functional features (roles, institutions, norms; adaptation, integration, pattern maintenance) and reproduce themselves through communication processes that create and maintain system–environment boundaries</cite>.

Systems-theoretic building blocks (what “elements” look like in practice)
- Boundary and perspective: Decide the unit of analysis (micro, meso, macro) and its scope; list what is inside vs. outside, including who counts as “elements” (agents, roles, institutions, infrastructures) and what exchanges cross the boundary (information, resources, risks). <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System boundaries must be explicit; elements include actors, interdependencies, hazards, exposed/vulnerable assets and people, governance, institutions, and policy-defined outcomes</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Boundaries distinguish inputs/outputs and internal/external elements</cite>.
- Components and components’ relations: Identify concrete elements (roles, institutions, networks, artifacts) and the relational couplings among them (e.g., flows of communication, authority, resources). <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Social systems include patterns and networks of individuals organized into groups and structures performing functions</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Roles and institutions are elements of the social system’s structure that shape appropriate behavior</cite>.
- Information, communication, and meaning: Communication is a primary process in social systems; meaning, selectivity, and interpretation filter exchanges and sustain system identity. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">Meaningful utterances received by others and conveying information are necessary; a social system emerges when communication develops from communicative acts</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Mechanisms of self-regulation include adaptation, regulation, and transformation via processes that respond to internal tensions and external influences</cite>.
- Structure and pattern: Patterns of expectations, norms, and roles organize action and provide a scaffold for coordination; these are elements that emerge from and constrain interaction. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Pattern variables structure interaction systems by offering solutions to dilemmas of action; positions and roles are parts of the social system that express patterns of expectations, connecting individual action to the social whole</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Normative structure (rules, laws, moral norms, values) regulates behavior and is a core element alongside structure (roles, institutions, interactions)</cite>.
- Functions and subsystems: Social systems maintain life-sustaining functions (adaptation, goal attainment, integration, pattern maintenance) via specialized subsystems (e.g., economy, politics, law, culture) that are interdependent. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">The social interaction system has functional needs: adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, and latency/pattern maintenance (AGIL), with each function potentially fulfilled by distinct subsystems</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Commonly distinguished subsystems include economic, political, legal, cultural, and social, which perform specific functions while being closely interdependent</cite>.
- Openness, feedback, and dynamics: Boundaries exist for exchange; flows trigger feedbacks that regulate behavior, sustain or transform structures, and enable learning and adaptation. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Systems evolve through continuous interaction with environments and correct course via feedback</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Self-regulating systems are those that are self-correcting through feedback; systems theory integrates across levels and disciplines and emphasizes interconnected wholes over isolated components</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Mechanisms of self-regulation include adaptation, regulation, and transformation processes that respond to internal and external influences</cite>.
- Context and environment: Exogenous conditions (e.g., technologies, markets, hazards, policies) and endogenous history shape feasible options, constraints, and equilibria. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definition includes identification of hazards and exposed/vulnerable elements, governance and institutions, and desired outcomes set by policy</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-0">Component–interaction frameworks emphasize how social systems organize exchanges and adapt in complex, dynamic settings</cite>.

Common element categories (integrative checklist)
- Structural elements: roles and statuses; institutions and organizations; positions in networks; hierarchies and authority schemas. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Positions and roles, as elements of the social system, express patterns of expectations and link individual action to the system</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Structure is a relatively stable pattern of social roles, institutions, and interactions between them</cite>.
- Relational elements: social ties and networks; exchange relations; interdependence and dependencies among subsystems. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Networks of individuals organized into groups and structures</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Interdependence between subsystems determines stability and vulnerability</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">Interdependencies among actors (e.g., households, firms, government) require delineation and assessment</cite>.
- Normative/value elements: norms, laws, moral codes, and shared meanings that regulate conduct and allocate rights/responsibilities. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Normative structure (rules, laws, moral norms, values) regulates behavior</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Patterns of expectations specify appropriate behavior and are elements of the social system’s structure</cite>.
- Informational/communicative elements: channels, codes, and media of communication; selection and interpretation; information flows that maintain system identity and boundary. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">Communication requires meaningful utterances received by others; society as thoroughly relational is constituted by communication processes</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Information and communication are central to self-regulation and system–environment boundary maintenance</cite>.
- Processual/regulatory elements: adaptation, learning, goal setting, coordination mechanisms, and feedback loops (cybernetic control). <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Systems course-correct based on feedback and continuously evolve through interaction with environments</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Mechanisms of self-regulation include adaptation, regulation, and transformation</cite>.
- Boundary and environmental interface elements: defined perimeters; inputs/outputs; environmental hazards, resources, and policy/governance linkages. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Boundaries distinguish inputs and outputs and define internal vs external elements</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definitions enumerate hazards, exposed elements, governance, and desired outcomes to frame boundaries and exchanges</cite>.

Processes and dynamics that organize elements
- Coupling and differentiation: Elements and subsystems differentiate functions and reproduce through selective coupling to information flows, sustaining system identity and enabling change. <cite id="d6be7ea0-4">Luhmann’s systemic approach emphasizes processual, diachronic functions and introduces structural coupling, situating individuals within contexts and analyzing functional specificity of communication</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">Communication processes create and maintain system–environment boundaries</cite>.
- Functional balance and disequilibrium: Systems tend to maintain functional balance (AGIL) while interdependencies create vulnerabilities and transformational pressures. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Each social system fulfills adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, and pattern maintenance needs, often via distinct subsystems</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Interdependence among subsystems determines stability and vulnerability under internal and external challenges</cite>.
- Open-systems metabolism: Continuous exchange with environments sustains structures and triggers adaptation via feedback; emergent phenomena (e.g., social movements, crises) reconfigure elements. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Continuous interaction with environments and feedback-driven course correction underlie evolution</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definitions integrate hazards, exposed elements, governance, and desired outcomes to capture environmental coupling and regulatory levers</cite>.
- Multi-level organization: Elements exist across micro/meso/macro levels and across domains (e.g., economy, politics), interacting across scales. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">Systems-of-systems approaches delineate subsystems at different geographical scales and actor types (households, firms, government) with interdependencies</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Subsystems (economic, political, legal, cultural) are interdependent across levels</cite>.

How perspectives differ and integrate
- Parsonsian structural-functionalist view: Systems are organized hierarchically by structure (roles, norms, patterns) to fulfill AGIL functions; this emphasizes stability and functional interdependence. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Pattern variables structure interactions; roles and norms express system-level expectations; AGIL functions guide subsystem specialization</cite>.
- Luhmann’s communication theory: Systems are best understood as codependent networks of communications that reproduce themselves; individuals are not elements of the social system but become involved via selective coupling to communications. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">A social system emerges when communication develops from communicative acts; individuals are not included as elements, underscoring society’s relational constitution</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-4">Luhmann de-emphasizes the actor as primary motivational center; social conflict arises contingently in communicative events, with structural coupling enabling system-specific functions</cite>.
- General systems theory framing: Provides boundary, component, relation, feedback, and environment tools used across social systems analysis; stresses openness, equifinality, and interdisciplinary integration. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Systems are complex networks interacting with environments and correcting via feedback; social systems are exemplars of such organization</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-3">All phenomena are webs of relationships among elements; systems are “elements in standing relationship”</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Systems are coherent entities with inputs/outputs and boundaries; GST integrates across disciplines and emphasizes interconnected wholes</cite>.
- Complexity and CAS perspectives: Focus on nonlinearity, adaptation, and emergent macro-level phenomena from micro-level interactions; elements and interdependencies are central constructs. <cite id="4db2cf77-0">Component–interaction frameworks are used to capture how social systems organize and adapt in complex, dynamic settings like fission–fusion dynamics</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-3">Operational frameworks define unit systems, interdependence profiles, and social impact assessments to analyze how elements interact</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical way to define and inventory elements
- Start with a clear system definition: boundary, purpose, and unit of analysis; enumerate what is inside and what counts as exchange with the environment. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">Explicit system boundaries and identification of hazards, exposed elements, governance, and desired outcomes provide clarity</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Boundaries and input–output flows distinguish internal from external elements</cite>.
- Enumerate structural elements: roles/statuses, institutions/organizations, and stable interaction patterns that regulate behavior. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Roles and institutions as elements of structure express patterns of expectations</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Structure comprises roles, institutions, and interaction patterns</cite>.
- Map relational elements: networks, interdependencies, and flows of resources, information, and power across and within subsystems. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Social systems include networks of individuals organized into groups and structures</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Interdependence among subsystems shapes stability and vulnerability</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-3">Interdependence profiling clarifies how subsystems depend on one another</cite>.
- Specify normative/value elements: codified and informal rules, norms, and meanings that allocate rights, obligations, and preferences in coordination. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Normative structure regulates behavior</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Pattern variables and role expectations encode appropriate behavior</cite>.
- Identify informational/communicative elements: channels, codes, and feedback mechanisms that reproduce system identity and enable adaptation. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">Communication requires meaningful, received utterances; a social system emerges from communication</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Self-regulation relies on information flows and feedback</cite>.
- Note processual/regulatory elements: mechanisms of adaptation, learning, goal setting, and conflict/coordination that maintain or transform functions. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Mechanisms include adaptation, regulation, and transformation in response to tensions and influences</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-4">Structural coupling and contingent communicative events generate transformational processes</cite>.
- Contextualize with environment and history: list exogenous hazards, policies, markets, technologies, and social capital that shape system behavior and options. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definitions include hazards, exposed elements, governance, and policy outcomes</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Continuous interaction with environments and feedback underlies evolution</cite>.

Illustrative examples
- Corporate organization: elements include employees and managers (roles), hierarchies and departments (structure), internal memos and meetings (communication), performance norms and codes of conduct (norms), resource flows and budgets (relations), feedback loops via KPIs and audits (regulation), and market, legal, and technological environments (context). <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Organizations are complex networks of interacting elements that interact with environments and use feedback to evolve</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Roles and norms structure appropriate behavior and connect individual action to the system</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Subsystems (e.g., HR, finance) interdependently perform functions like adaptation and goal attainment</cite>.
- Urban risk governance: elements include residents and agencies (roles), emergency services and regulators (institutions), communication networks and sirens (information), formal rules and community norms (normative), interdependencies among households, insurers, and government (relations), feedback via drills and incident reviews (regulation), and environmental hazards like floods and terrorism (context). <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definition delineates boundaries, actors, interdependencies, hazards, exposed elements, governance, and desired outcomes</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Subsystems (economy, politics, law, culture) interdependently perform functions and are vulnerable due to interdependence</cite>.

Summary
- Coherent definition: a social system is a boundary-delineated, open organization of interrelated social elements—people, roles, institutions, meanings, and communications—whose reciprocal relations produce emergent, functionally organized structures and processes that regulate adaptation and reproduction in a given environment. <cite id="4db2cf77-1">A social system is a whole of interrelated social elements</cite> <cite id="a9e788e1-4">with discernible boundaries and input–output flows</cite> <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">whose roles and norms encode patterns of expectation</cite> <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">and whose communication processes create and maintain system boundaries</cite> <cite id="a9e788e1-0">and evolve through environment interaction and feedback</cite>.
- Essential elements: structure (roles/institutions/patterns), relations (networks/interdependencies), norms/meaning (values and rules), information/communication (channels and interpretation), processes (adaptation/learning/feedback), and context/environment (hazards, governance, policies). <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Structure, functions (AGIL), normative structures, and mechanisms of self-regulation</cite> <cite id="a9e788e1-0">plus evolving component–environment exchanges</cite> <cite id="4db2cf77-4">with explicit boundary-setting and environmental hazards, governance, and outcomes</cite>.
- Unifying lens: general systems theory provides tools (boundary, components, relations, feedback, levels) while sociological traditions add concrete social content (roles, norms, AGIL functions, communicative reproduction), yielding a practical, integrative framework for defining and analyzing social systems. <cite id="a9e788e1-3">Systems are “elements in standing relationship”</cite> <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">and are analytically decomposed into roles, norms, and functional needs</cite> <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">with communication as the constitutive process</cite> <cite id="a9e788e1-4">and openness to environment via feedback</cite>.

Snippet: Explicitly defining the system boundaries and its internal complex networks of interdependencies is needed for tackling these challenges. 

In this article, we define a system as a set of (partly) interconnected elements with clear boundaries. In addition, we define system of systems as a system in which its elements can again be seen as systems. Figure 2 introduces an example of a system and system elements and shows a possible system of systems approach based on different geographical scales and possible actors involved. These key concepts, i.e., systems, systems elements, and systems of systems, are depicted in Figure 3. To provide a clearer understanding of the framework, Figure 2 illustrates the differentiation between elements on different system levels. To further demonstrate the application of the framework, we present a conceptual example in Figures 3 and 4, which includes households, an insurance provider, and the government as possible systems. 

Another crucial step in understanding systems is identifying current and/or future challenges for the system holder (e.g., the government, a specific sector, etc.) through engaging with a specific sustainability iScience Perspective challenge (e.g., resilience to multi-hazards of interconnected countries with strong macroeconomic relationships, disaster resilience of islands with strong economic dependence on tourism, etc.). 2 Given that the framework is focused on natural-hazard related risks, a system definition also includes the identification of hazards of interest and associated hazard scenarios (including both single and multi-hazards), as well as the identification of exposed and vulnerable elements of the system (e.g., assets and people located in hazard-prone areas together with different dimensions of vulnerability, such as economic, social, institutional, physical, etc.). Different natural hazards of interest can be identified together with their interrelationships 15,25,26,30 (as presented in Section Muti-hazards, multi-risks, and systemic risk: A brief overview). 

A system definition also requires an understanding of the existing governance landscape (i.e., main policies, institutions, and stakeholders guiding the system), including understanding the gaps that contribute to the sustainability challenges identified. This can help in, for instance, defining what a desired outcome for the system is as defined in a specific policy (e.g., sectoral policies, disaster risk management policies).

Luhmann's system theory departs from Parsons's postulation. While Parsons tends to deem system as having steady properties because it is founded upon mutual consensus, Luhmann sees it differently. He thinks that the nature of system is relatively unstable, owing to the fact that a system is not built upon consensus, rather it is built by and upon social interaction. The concept of social interaction also covers the concepts of conflict and social change -something that Parsons had failed to recognise. The recognition of social interaction concept affirms that Luhmann's concept prioritises function more than it prioritises structure. 23 neer and Nassehi, as cited by Hardiman, identified three points of modification that Luhmann had made to Parsons's concept. The first modification is, that social systems are not founded upon norms structure or other certain structure that dominate the society, rather, it is founded upon social interaction. This thought finds its root from the complexity of problems (norms and other) in the society. Luhmann saw a system from its presence compared to other social systems. This point of view is distinct from Parsons's, who deemed that social system exists singularly for itself. 

The second modification is the attitude towards Parsons's theory, which says that a system will collapse if certain systemic functions are disturbed. Luhmann presented that social systems can replace the damaged functions with alternative functions, thereby assuring the system to keep operating. 24 e third modification relates with the maintenance and sustainability of social system. For Parsons, the highest social unit is social system, therefore there is nothing outside social system. Luhmann reached another formulation: that the highest social unit is the world (Welt), therefore the existence of a social system is relative if compared to the other social systems.
</snippet>

A social system is a way of defining certain relations between the components of 'action' that specifically relate to this reality (Parsons, 1970, p. 839). In the concept of social system, the mutual interactions of individuals are comprised, but perceived from the side of the structure of this interdependence, i.e. certain 'emergent' properties to which the system as a whole is entitled, with the interrelated interactions as a foundation. From the point of view of the properties of the social system as a whole, the orientations and actions of individuals are expressed in terms of position and role, i.e. their place in the structure of social relations and normatively regulated behaviour. In this respect, Parsons states clearly that the position and role are not attributes of empirically given subjects of action, but primarily parts of the social system that should be theoretically expressed in this form. Hence, the social system does not include the individual subject of action, understood as a concrete system of action, but only a part of the latter, expressed in the concept of role. Yet, the role has the function of an element connecting the action system of the individual subject with the social system (Parsons, Shils, 1959, p. 190;Parsons, 1965, p. 42). However, from the point of view of the social system, a role is an element in the general pattern that determines the action of the individuals that make up the system. In other words, an essential aspect of the social structure is a system framed in patterns of expectations that determine the appropriate behaviour of individuals performing certain roles (Parsons, 1972, p. 307). 

The social interaction system as a whole has, according to Parsons, its own functional needs. He lists four basic needs: adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, latency or pattern maintenance (the so-called AGIL model). At the most general level of a social system, each function is fulfilled by a distinct sub-system, each of which also has a similar structure of functional needs.
</snippet>

Title: Dysfunctions and Transformational Processes in Social Systems under Contemporary Global Changes
Snippet: Among these, the economic, political, legal, cultural, and social subsystems are most commonly distinguished. Each of them performs specific functions while remaining closely connected with the others and influencing their functioning. This interdependence between subsystems determines both the stability and the vulnerability of social systems in the face of internal and external challenges. 

Every social system is characterized by certain structural and functional features that determine the way it operates and develops. These include: − Structurea relatively stable pattern of social roles, institutions, and interactions between them; 

− Functionsactivities and processes aimed at satisfying the fundamental needs of society and its members; 

− Normative structurea system of rules, laws, moral norms, and values that regulate the behavior of individuals and groups; 

− Mechanisms of self-regulationprocesses of adaptation, regulation, and transformation that enable the system to respond to internal tensions and external influences. 

The development of the systems approach in the social sciences is closely associated with the theoretical contributions of a number of scholars. A particularly significant contribution in this field is the structuralfunctional theory of the American sociologist Talcott Parsons. According to his concept, society represents a system of interacting subsystems that must fulfill certain functional requirements in order to ensure the stability and sustainability of the social order. Parsons formulated four fundamental functions that every social system must perform: adaptation, goal attainment, integration, and latency (pattern maintenance). This model, known as the AGIL framework, emphasizes the necessity of maintaining functional balance among the different elements of the social system. 

Further development of social systems theory can be observed in the works of the German sociologist Niklas Luhmann, who proposed a different interpretation of social reality. According to his theory, society can be understood as a system of communications rather than merely a collection of individuals or institutions. Social systems, according to Luhmann, reproduce themselves through continuous communication processes that create and maintain the boundary between the system and its environment. This perspective directs attention to the role of information, communication, and interpretation in processes of social interaction. 

Despite the differences between various theoretical approaches, most scholars agree that social systems possess a number of common characteristics that define their nature and mode of functioning. Among the most important characteristics are: 

− Opennesssocial systems actively interact with their external environment and exchange resources, information, and energy;
</snippet>

Title: Conflict, Fear, and War as Constitutive Dimensions of Social Order
Snippet: Luhmann's social systems theory may be regarded as an alternative perspective to classical theory and the conceptual frameworks of advanced modernity developed by Marx, Weber, and Parsons, particularly with respect to the dichotomous pair integrationism/conflictualism. 

Luhmann's approach represents a departure from the conception of conflict inherent in Marxist thought. It posits that social conflict arises from communicative events that are contingent and highly improbable. This stands in contrast to Marxian theory, which, viewing the evolution of social systems through a conflictual lens, suggests that outcomes are largely predetermined. By contrast, Luhmann treats the evolution of social systems probabilistically, highlighting the contingent and highly improbable conditions of social reality. While in the Weberian model individuals exist within a social system as a unified entity, Luhmann's conceptual framework presents a desubjectivized perspective, de-emphasizing the role of the social actor as the primary motivational and intentional centre of social action. Rather, it is individual actions that shape one's involvement in specific social systems. 

Rivista Italiana di Filosofia Politica 9 (2025): 233-251 Gianpasquale Preite, Riccardo Zappatore Luhmann's systemic approach transcends the ontological challenge inherent in the concept of society by acknowledging the existence of social entities that maintain their own identities, thereby affirming their status as systems. This perspective also marks a departure from the Parsonsian framework, which perceives structure as fixed and synchronous. In contrast, Luhmann assigns a crucial role to the dynamic, processual, and diachronic nature of functions. With the publication of Soziale Systeme in 1984, he definitively revised Parsons's conception of the relationship between systems by introducing the notion of structural coupling. This framework overcomes the asymmetry of the Parsonsian model by situating the individual within their social context, thereby enabling the analysis of the functional specificity of communication within systems and the capacity of psychic systems to produce knowledge through communication.

Title: The quest for innovation: learning systems and innovativeness within a global staffing organization.
Snippet: General systems theory was outlined in 1969 by Ludwig von Bertalanffy who researched the organization of complex systems and provides a set of logical assertions about causality in organizations. Von Bertalanffy (1969) believed a system to be a complex network of interacting elements that continuously interact with their environments. Through this interaction, they transform and thus continuously evolve. Von Bertalanffy (1969) also believed these systems course-correct based on feedback. Building upon general systems theory, social systems include patterns and networks of individuals from various origins or statuses that roll into groups or structures that carry out diverse functions.

Title: Social relations: Building on Ludwig von Bertalanffy
Snippet: Ludwig von Bertalanffy did not leave us a legacy of a social systems theory. Nonetheless, reconstructing his general approach to systems provides us with several ideas on how to build a theory of social systems. The concept of social relations easily connects to Bertalanffy's concept of relations of organization. His way of thinking underlines that social relations, as any relations of organization, are unobservables that long for theoretical means of understanding. His conception of the world would assign social relations a special place in a hierarchy of processes internal to a social system — they represent the whole of the sys-tem that nonetheless emerges from the interaction of the actors as parts thereof. Last but not least, his world view would orient us towards an organization of social systems in which the dialectic of social relations and actors balances unity and diversity as an Ought. These three main ideas of Bertalanffy offer system theoretical pillars that can inspire current social theory.
</snippet>

Title: On the history of Ludwig von Bertalanffy’s “General Systemology”, and on its relationship to cybernetics – part III: convergences and divergences
Snippet: Bertalanffy’s so-called “general system theory” (GST) and cybernetics were and are often confused: this calls for clarification. In this article, Bertalanffy’s conceptions and ideas are compared with those developed in cybernetics in order to investigate the differences and convergences. Bertalanffy was concerned with first order cybernetics. Nonetheless, his perspectivist epistemology is also relevant with regard to developments in second order cybernetics, and the latter is therefore also considered to some extent. W. Ross Ashby’s important role as mediator between GST and cybernetics is analysed. The respective basic epistemological approaches, scientific approaches and inherent world views are discussed. We underline the complementarity of cybernetic and “organismic” trends in systems research within the unitary hermeneutical framework of “general systemology”.
</snippet>

Snippet: This study is anchored on the Systems Theory as propounded by Ludwig von Bertalanffy. Systems theory is the interdisciplinary study of systems in general, with the goal of elucidating principles that can be applied to all types of systems at all nesting levels in all fields of research. The term originates from Bertalanffy's General System Theory (GST) and is used in later efforts in other fields, such as the action theory of Talcott Parsons and the social systems theory of Niklas Luhmann. In this context the word systems is used to refer specifically to self-regulating systems, i.e. that are selfcorrecting through feedback. Self-regulating systems are found in nature, including the physiological systems of our body, in local and global ecosystems, and in climate-and in human learning processes (Von Bertalanffy, 1968). 

As a transdisciplinary, interdisciplinary and multiperspectival domain, the area brings together principles and concepts from ontology, philosophy of science, physics, computer science, biology, and engineering as well as geography, sociology, political science, psychotherapy (within family systems therapy) and economics among others. Systems theory thus serves as a bridge for interdisciplinary dialogue between autonomous areas of study as well as within the area of systems science itself. Systems theory became the name used by early investigators for the interdependence of relationships created in organizations by defining a new way of thinking about science and scientific paradigms. System in this frame of reference is composed of regularly interacting or interrelating groups of activities. 

The systems view is a world-view that is based on the discipline of System Inquiry. Central to systems inquiry is the concept of SYSTEM. In the most general sense, system means a configuration of parts connected and joined together by a web of relationships. The Primer group defines system as a family of relationships among the members acting as a whole. Von Bertalanffy (1968) defined system as "elements in standing relationship" (Von Bertalanffy, 1968). The systems view was based on several fundamental ideas. First, all phenomena can be viewed as a web of relationships among elements, or a system.
</snippet>

Snippet: Bertalanffy, (1972), a German scientist, introduced systems theory in the 1930s at a philosophy seminar at the University of Chicago. Initially developed in the context of life sciences, systems theory has evolved into the modern field of ecology. He defined a system as a coherent entity with discernible boundaries, distinguishing internal and external elements and identifying input and output relationships (Bertalanffy, 1972). Systems theory is a theoretical perspective that analyses phenomena as an interconnected wholes rather than as isolated components. Lai, (2017) believed that understanding a system required examining its interconnected components rather than isolating individual parts. In his work "General Systems Theory: Essays on Its Foundation and Development," by Bertalanffy outlines the objectives of systems theory as: (1) integration of various sciences, (2) development of a general theory of systems, (3) advancement of exact theory in non-physical fields, (4) establishment of unifying principles across different sciences, and (5) integration of scientific education (Bertalanffy, 1972). While systems theory was not originally intended for applications in communication, family studies, or applied science, it has proven valuable in understanding the systems of the world around us. Through systems theory, we can gain a deeper understanding of the world and explore problems and their underlying causes (Bertalanffy, 1972;Khuzwayo, 2020). 

Systems can be found in nature, science, society, economics, and information systems (Larsson et al., 2010). A distinctive characteristic of systems theories is their simultaneous development across various disciplines. Scholars working from a systems theory perspective often build upon knowledge and concepts developed within other fields. Examples included natural and ecological sciences, with concepts such as organic aspects, homeostasis, and equifinality. 

Additionally, systems theory can also be used to develop and evaluate effective environmental policies and interventions by considering the interconnectedness of different environmental factors (Leydesdorff, 1996). This view correlates with this study which examines the road safety environment. This includes safety strategies, mediating human, environmental, vehicle, and road infrastructure factors in a coherent manner to ensure the utmost safety of the road.

Below is a concise, evidence-backed definition of social systems and their core elements, synthesized across classical sociological theory, general systems theory, and contemporary systems-of-practice perspectives.

Definition and scope
- A social system is a purposive whole formed by a set of interrelated social elements—people, roles, institutions, meanings, and actions—whose reciprocal relations produce emergent properties that cannot be reduced to any single element alone. <cite id="4db2cf77-1">A system is a whole of elements or parts that are related to one another in a unit; when applied to society, a social system is a whole of social elements that are related and influence each other</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">A social system is not an empirically given concrete reality but a theoretical model that defines certain relations between components of action; from the system’s perspective, orientation and action are expressed in position and role and in patterns of expectations that determine appropriate behavior</cite>.
- Social systems are open, boundary-delineated organizations of interacting parts coupled to environments from which they take inputs and to which they export outputs via flows of matter, energy, information, and feedback. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">A system is a complex network of interacting elements that continuously interact with their environments, transform and evolve, and course-correct based on feedback; social systems include patterns and networks of individuals in groups and structures that carry out diverse functions</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">A system is a coherent entity with discernible boundaries distinguishing internal and external elements and identifying input–output relationships</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">Explicitly defining system boundaries and internal networks of interdependencies is crucial; systems can be composed of subsystems (e.g., households, firms, government), with identified hazards, exposed elements, governance/institutions, and desired outcomes</cite>.
- As complex adaptive and relational entities, social systems are often analyzed as sets of interdependent components that self-organize and reproduce through interactions, creating and maintaining system distinctions (self/other, inside/outside). <cite id="4db2cf77-0">In complex adaptive systems, “components” and “interactions” are operative; social systems exhibiting fission–fusion dynamics can be framed by defining components and their interactions</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">A social system emerges when communication develops from communicative acts; society is relational without including human individuals as elements of the system itself, emphasizing that meaningful utterances received by others and conveying meaningful information are necessary for communication</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Social systems are characterized by structural and functional features (roles, institutions, norms; adaptation, integration, pattern maintenance) and reproduce themselves through communication processes that create and maintain system–environment boundaries</cite>.

Systems-theoretic building blocks (what “elements” look like in practice)
- Boundary and perspective: Decide the unit of analysis (micro, meso, macro) and its scope; list what is inside vs. outside, including who counts as “elements” (agents, roles, institutions, infrastructures) and what exchanges cross the boundary (information, resources, risks). <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System boundaries must be explicit; elements include actors, interdependencies, hazards, exposed/vulnerable assets and people, governance, institutions, and policy-defined outcomes</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Boundaries distinguish inputs/outputs and internal/external elements</cite>.
- Components and components’ relations: Identify concrete elements (roles, institutions, networks, artifacts) and the relational couplings among them (e.g., flows of communication, authority, resources). <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Social systems include patterns and networks of individuals organized into groups and structures performing functions</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Roles and institutions are elements of the social system’s structure that shape appropriate behavior</cite>.
- Information, communication, and meaning: Communication is a primary process in social systems; meaning, selectivity, and interpretation filter exchanges and sustain system identity. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">Meaningful utterances received by others and conveying information are necessary; a social system emerges when communication develops from communicative acts</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Mechanisms of self-regulation include adaptation, regulation, and transformation via processes that respond to internal tensions and external influences</cite>.
- Structure and pattern: Patterns of expectations, norms, and roles organize action and provide a scaffold for coordination; these are elements that emerge from and constrain interaction. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Pattern variables structure interaction systems by offering solutions to dilemmas of action; positions and roles are parts of the social system that express patterns of expectations, connecting individual action to the social whole</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Normative structure (rules, laws, moral norms, values) regulates behavior and is a core element alongside structure (roles, institutions, interactions)</cite>.
- Functions and subsystems: Social systems maintain life-sustaining functions (adaptation, goal attainment, integration, pattern maintenance) via specialized subsystems (e.g., economy, politics, law, culture) that are interdependent. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">The social interaction system has functional needs: adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, and latency/pattern maintenance (AGIL), with each function potentially fulfilled by distinct subsystems</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Commonly distinguished subsystems include economic, political, legal, cultural, and social, which perform specific functions while being closely interdependent</cite>.
- Openness, feedback, and dynamics: Boundaries exist for exchange; flows trigger feedbacks that regulate behavior, sustain or transform structures, and enable learning and adaptation. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Systems evolve through continuous interaction with environments and correct course via feedback</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Self-regulating systems are those that are self-correcting through feedback; systems theory integrates across levels and disciplines and emphasizes interconnected wholes over isolated components</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Mechanisms of self-regulation include adaptation, regulation, and transformation processes that respond to internal and external influences</cite>.
- Context and environment: Exogenous conditions (e.g., technologies, markets, hazards, policies) and endogenous history shape feasible options, constraints, and equilibria. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definition includes identification of hazards and exposed/vulnerable elements, governance and institutions, and desired outcomes set by policy</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-0">Component–interaction frameworks emphasize how social systems organize exchanges and adapt in complex, dynamic settings</cite>.

Common element categories (integrative checklist)
- Structural elements: roles and statuses; institutions and organizations; positions in networks; hierarchies and authority schemas. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Positions and roles, as elements of the social system, express patterns of expectations and link individual action to the system</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Structure is a relatively stable pattern of social roles, institutions, and interactions between them</cite>.
- Relational elements: social ties and networks; exchange relations; interdependence and dependencies among subsystems. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Networks of individuals organized into groups and structures</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Interdependence between subsystems determines stability and vulnerability</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">Interdependencies among actors (e.g., households, firms, government) require delineation and assessment</cite>.
- Normative/value elements: norms, laws, moral codes, and shared meanings that regulate conduct and allocate rights/responsibilities. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Normative structure (rules, laws, moral norms, values) regulates behavior</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Patterns of expectations specify appropriate behavior and are elements of the social system’s structure</cite>.
- Informational/communicative elements: channels, codes, and media of communication; selection and interpretation; information flows that maintain system identity and boundary. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">Communication requires meaningful utterances received by others; society as thoroughly relational is constituted by communication processes</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Information and communication are central to self-regulation and system–environment boundary maintenance</cite>.
- Processual/regulatory elements: adaptation, learning, goal setting, coordination mechanisms, and feedback loops (cybernetic control). <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Systems course-correct based on feedback and continuously evolve through interaction with environments</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Mechanisms of self-regulation include adaptation, regulation, and transformation</cite>.
- Boundary and environmental interface elements: defined perimeters; inputs/outputs; environmental hazards, resources, and policy/governance linkages. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Boundaries distinguish inputs and outputs and define internal vs external elements</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definitions enumerate hazards, exposed elements, governance, and desired outcomes to frame boundaries and exchanges</cite>.

Processes and dynamics that organize elements
- Coupling and differentiation: Elements and subsystems differentiate functions and reproduce through selective coupling to information flows, sustaining system identity and enabling change. <cite id="d6be7ea0-4">Luhmann’s systemic approach emphasizes processual, diachronic functions and introduces structural coupling, situating individuals within contexts and analyzing functional specificity of communication</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">Communication processes create and maintain system–environment boundaries</cite>.
- Functional balance and disequilibrium: Systems tend to maintain functional balance (AGIL) while interdependencies create vulnerabilities and transformational pressures. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Each social system fulfills adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, and pattern maintenance needs, often via distinct subsystems</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Interdependence among subsystems determines stability and vulnerability under internal and external challenges</cite>.
- Open-systems metabolism: Continuous exchange with environments sustains structures and triggers adaptation via feedback; emergent phenomena (e.g., social movements, crises) reconfigure elements. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Continuous interaction with environments and feedback-driven course correction underlie evolution</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definitions integrate hazards, exposed elements, governance, and desired outcomes to capture environmental coupling and regulatory levers</cite>.
- Multi-level organization: Elements exist across micro/meso/macro levels and across domains (e.g., economy, politics), interacting across scales. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">Systems-of-systems approaches delineate subsystems at different geographical scales and actor types (households, firms, government) with interdependencies</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Subsystems (economic, political, legal, cultural) are interdependent across levels</cite>.

How perspectives differ and integrate
- Parsonsian structural-functionalist view: Systems are organized hierarchically by structure (roles, norms, patterns) to fulfill AGIL functions; this emphasizes stability and functional interdependence. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Pattern variables structure interactions; roles and norms express system-level expectations; AGIL functions guide subsystem specialization</cite>.
- Luhmann’s communication theory: Systems are best understood as codependent networks of communications that reproduce themselves; individuals are not elements of the social system but become involved via selective coupling to communications. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">A social system emerges when communication develops from communicative acts; individuals are not included as elements, underscoring society’s relational constitution</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-4">Luhmann de-emphasizes the actor as primary motivational center; social conflict arises contingently in communicative events, with structural coupling enabling system-specific functions</cite>.
- General systems theory framing: Provides boundary, component, relation, feedback, and environment tools used across social systems analysis; stresses openness, equifinality, and interdisciplinary integration. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Systems are complex networks interacting with environments and correcting via feedback; social systems are exemplars of such organization</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-3">All phenomena are webs of relationships among elements; systems are “elements in standing relationship”</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Systems are coherent entities with inputs/outputs and boundaries; GST integrates across disciplines and emphasizes interconnected wholes</cite>.
- Complexity and CAS perspectives: Focus on nonlinearity, adaptation, and emergent macro-level phenomena from micro-level interactions; elements and interdependencies are central constructs. <cite id="4db2cf77-0">Component–interaction frameworks are used to capture how social systems organize and adapt in complex, dynamic settings like fission–fusion dynamics</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-3">Operational frameworks define unit systems, interdependence profiles, and social impact assessments to analyze how elements interact</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical way to define and inventory elements
- Start with a clear system definition: boundary, purpose, and unit of analysis; enumerate what is inside and what counts as exchange with the environment. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">Explicit system boundaries and identification of hazards, exposed elements, governance, and desired outcomes provide clarity</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-4">Boundaries and input–output flows distinguish internal from external elements</cite>.
- Enumerate structural elements: roles/statuses, institutions/organizations, and stable interaction patterns that regulate behavior. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Roles and institutions as elements of structure express patterns of expectations</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Structure comprises roles, institutions, and interaction patterns</cite>.
- Map relational elements: networks, interdependencies, and flows of resources, information, and power across and within subsystems. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Social systems include networks of individuals organized into groups and structures</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Interdependence among subsystems shapes stability and vulnerability</cite>. <cite id="4db2cf77-3">Interdependence profiling clarifies how subsystems depend on one another</cite>.
- Specify normative/value elements: codified and informal rules, norms, and meanings that allocate rights, obligations, and preferences in coordination. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Normative structure regulates behavior</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Pattern variables and role expectations encode appropriate behavior</cite>.
- Identify informational/communicative elements: channels, codes, and feedback mechanisms that reproduce system identity and enable adaptation. <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">Communication requires meaningful, received utterances; a social system emerges from communication</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Self-regulation relies on information flows and feedback</cite>.
- Note processual/regulatory elements: mechanisms of adaptation, learning, goal setting, and conflict/coordination that maintain or transform functions. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Mechanisms include adaptation, regulation, and transformation in response to tensions and influences</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-4">Structural coupling and contingent communicative events generate transformational processes</cite>.
- Contextualize with environment and history: list exogenous hazards, policies, markets, technologies, and social capital that shape system behavior and options. <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definitions include hazards, exposed elements, governance, and policy outcomes</cite>. <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Continuous interaction with environments and feedback underlies evolution</cite>.

Illustrative examples
- Corporate organization: elements include employees and managers (roles), hierarchies and departments (structure), internal memos and meetings (communication), performance norms and codes of conduct (norms), resource flows and budgets (relations), feedback loops via KPIs and audits (regulation), and market, legal, and technological environments (context). <cite id="a9e788e1-0">Organizations are complex networks of interacting elements that interact with environments and use feedback to evolve</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">Roles and norms structure appropriate behavior and connect individual action to the system</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Subsystems (e.g., HR, finance) interdependently perform functions like adaptation and goal attainment</cite>.
- Urban risk governance: elements include residents and agencies (roles), emergency services and regulators (institutions), communication networks and sirens (information), formal rules and community norms (normative), interdependencies among households, insurers, and government (relations), feedback via drills and incident reviews (regulation), and environmental hazards like floods and terrorism (context). <cite id="4db2cf77-4">System definition delineates boundaries, actors, interdependencies, hazards, exposed elements, governance, and desired outcomes</cite>. <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Subsystems (economy, politics, law, culture) interdependently perform functions and are vulnerable due to interdependence</cite>.

Summary
- Coherent definition: a social system is a boundary-delineated, open organization of interrelated social elements—people, roles, institutions, meanings, and communications—whose reciprocal relations produce emergent, functionally organized structures and processes that regulate adaptation and reproduction in a given environment. <cite id="4db2cf77-1">A social system is a whole of interrelated social elements</cite> <cite id="a9e788e1-4">with discernible boundaries and input–output flows</cite> <cite id="d6be7ea0-2">whose roles and norms encode patterns of expectation</cite> <cite id="d6be7ea0-1">and whose communication processes create and maintain system boundaries</cite> <cite id="a9e788e1-0">and evolve through environment interaction and feedback</cite>.
- Essential elements: structure (roles/institutions/patterns), relations (networks/interdependencies), norms/meaning (values and rules), information/communication (channels and interpretation), processes (adaptation/learning/feedback), and context/environment (hazards, governance, policies). <cite id="d6be7ea0-3">Structure, functions (AGIL), normative structures, and mechanisms of self-regulation</cite> <cite id="a9e788e1-0">plus evolving component–environment exchanges</cite> <cite id="4db2cf77-4">with explicit boundary-setting and environmental hazards, governance, and outcomes</cite>.

In this article, we define a system as a set of (partly) interconnected elements with clear boundaries. These key concepts, i.e., systems, systems elements, and systems of systems, are depicted in Figure 3. To provide a clearer understanding of the framework, Figure 2 illustrates the differentiation between elements on different system levels. To further demonstrate the application of the framework, we present a conceptual example in Figures 3 and 4, which includes households, an insurance provider, and the government as possible systems. 

Another crucial step in understanding systems is identifying current and/or future challenges for the system holder (e.g., the government, a specific sector, etc.) through engaging with a specific sustainability iScience Perspective challenge (e.g., resilience to multi-hazards of interconnected countries with strong macroeconomic relationships, disaster resilience of islands with strong economic dependence on tourism, etc.). 2 Given that the framework is focused on natural-hazard related risks, a system definition also includes the identification of hazards of interest and associated hazard scenarios (including both single and multi-hazards), as well as the identification of exposed and vulnerable elements of the system (e.g., assets and people located in hazard-prone areas together with different dimensions of vulnerability, such as economic, social, institutional, physical, etc.). Different natural hazards of interest can be identified together with their interrelationships 15,25,26,30 (as presented in Section Muti-hazards, multi-risks, and systemic risk: A brief overview). 

A system definition also requires an understanding of the existing governance landscape (i.e., main policies, institutions, and stakeholders guiding the system), including understanding the gaps that contribute to the sustainability challenges identified. This can help in, for instance, defining what a desired outcome for the system is as defined in a specific policy (e.g., sectoral policies, disaster risk management policies).

Luhmann's system theory departs from Parsons's postulation. While Parsons tends to deem system as having steady properties because it is founded upon mutual consensus, Luhmann sees it differently. He thinks that the nature of system is relatively unstable, owing to the fact that a system is not built upon consensus, rather it is built by and upon social interaction. The concept of social interaction also covers the concepts of conflict and social change -something that Parsons had failed to recognise. The recognition of social interaction concept affirms that Luhmann's concept prioritises function more than it prioritises structure. 23 neer and Nassehi, as cited by Hardiman, identified three points of modification that Luhmann had made to Parsons's concept. The first modification is, that social systems are not founded upon norms structure or other certain structure that dominate the society, rather, it is founded upon social interaction. This thought finds its root from the complexity of problems (norms and other) in the society. Luhmann saw a system from its presence compared to other social systems. This point of view is distinct from Parsons's, who deemed that social system exists singularly for itself. 

The second modification is the attitude towards Parsons's theory, which says that a system will collapse if certain systemic functions are disturbed. Title: Disputes over the concept of social system and the critique of sociological reason
Snippet: The pattern variables structure the interaction system by offering solutions to the dilemmas of social action (Parsons, 1966, p. 59-66). 

The social system, however, is not an empirically given, concrete reality, but only a theoretical model of it. A social system is a way of defining certain relations between the components of 'action' that specifically relate to this reality (Parsons, 1970, p. 839). In the concept of social system, the mutual interactions of individuals are comprised, but perceived from the side of the structure of this interdependence, i.e. certain 'emergent' properties to which the system as a whole is entitled, with the interrelated interactions as a foundation. From the point of view of the properties of the social system as a whole, the orientations and actions of individuals are expressed in terms of position and role, i.e. their place in the structure of social relations and normatively regulated behaviour. In this respect, Parsons states clearly that the position and role are not attributes of empirically given subjects of action, but primarily parts of the social system that should be theoretically expressed in this form. Hence, the social system does not include the individual subject of action, understood as a concrete system of action, but only a part of the latter, expressed in the concept of role. Yet, the role has the function of an element connecting the action system of the individual subject with the social system (Parsons, Shils, 1959, p. 190;Parsons, 1965, p. 42). However, from the point of view of the social system, a role is an element in the general pattern that determines the action of the individuals that make up the system. In other words, an essential aspect of the social structure is a system framed in patterns of expectations that determine the appropriate behaviour of individuals performing certain roles (Parsons, 1972, p. 307). 

The social interaction system as a whole has, according to Parsons, its own functional needs. He lists four basic needs: adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, latency or pattern maintenance (the so-called AGIL model). At the most general level of a social system, each function is fulfilled by a distinct sub-system, each of which also has a similar structure of functional needs.

Title: Dysfunctions and Transformational Processes in Social Systems under Contemporary Global Changes
Snippet: Among these, the economic, political, legal, cultural, and social subsystems are most commonly distinguished. Each of them performs specific functions while remaining closely connected with the others and influencing their functioning. This interdependence between subsystems determines both the stability and the vulnerability of social systems in the face of internal and external challenges. 

Every social system is characterized by certain structural and functional features that determine the way it operates and develops. These include: − Structurea relatively stable pattern of social roles, institutions, and interactions between them; 

− Functionsactivities and processes aimed at satisfying the fundamental needs of society and its members; 

− Normative structurea system of rules, laws, moral norms, and values that regulate the behavior of individuals and groups; 

− Mechanisms of self-regulationprocesses of adaptation, regulation, and transformation that enable the system to respond to internal tensions and external influences. 

The development of the systems approach in the social sciences is closely associated with the theoretical contributions of a number of scholars. A particularly significant contribution in this field is the structuralfunctional theory of the American sociologist Talcott Parsons. According to his concept, society represents a system of interacting subsystems that must fulfill certain functional requirements in order to ensure the stability and sustainability of the social order. Parsons formulated four fundamental functions that every social system must perform: adaptation, goal attainment, integration, and latency (pattern maintenance). This model, known as the AGIL framework, emphasizes the necessity of maintaining functional balance among the different elements of the social system. 

Further development of social systems theory can be observed in the works of the German sociologist Niklas Luhmann, who proposed a different interpretation of social reality. According to his theory, society can be understood as a system of communications rather than merely a collection of individuals or institutions. Social systems, according to Luhmann, reproduce themselves through continuous communication processes that create and maintain the boundary between the system and its environment. This perspective directs attention to the role of information, communication, and interpretation in processes of social interaction. 

Despite the differences between various theoretical approaches, most scholars agree that social systems possess a number of common characteristics that define their nature and mode of functioning. Among the most important characteristics are: 

− Opennesssocial systems actively interact with their external environment and exchange resources, information, and energy;

Title: Conflict, Fear, and War as Constitutive Dimensions of Social Order
Snippet: Luhmann's social systems theory may be regarded as an alternative perspective to classical theory and the conceptual frameworks of advanced modernity developed by Marx, Weber, and Parsons, particularly with respect to the dichotomous pair integrationism/conflictualism. 

Luhmann's approach represents a departure from the conception of conflict inherent in Marxist thought. It posits that social conflict arises from communicative events that are contingent and highly improbable. This stands in contrast to Marxian theory, which, viewing the evolution of social systems through a conflictual lens, suggests that outcomes are largely predetermined. By contrast, Luhmann treats the evolution of social systems probabilistically, highlighting the contingent and highly improbable conditions of social reality. While in the Weberian model individuals exist within a social system as a unified entity, Luhmann's conceptual framework presents a desubjectivized perspective, de-emphasizing the role of the social actor as the primary motivational and intentional centre of social action. Rather, it is individual actions that shape one's involvement in specific social systems. 

Rivista Italiana di Filosofia Politica 9 (2025): 233-251 Gianpasquale Preite, Riccardo Zappatore Luhmann's systemic approach transcends the ontological challenge inherent in the concept of society by acknowledging the existence of social entities that maintain their own identities, thereby affirming their status as systems. This perspective also marks a departure from the Parsonsian framework, which perceives structure as fixed and synchronous. In contrast, Luhmann assigns a crucial role to the dynamic, processual, and diachronic nature of functions. With the publication of Soziale Systeme in 1984, he definitively revised Parsons's conception of the relationship between systems by introducing the notion of structural coupling. This framework overcomes the asymmetry of the Parsonsian model by situating the individual within their social context, thereby enabling the analysis of the functional specificity of communication within systems and the capacity of psychic systems to produce knowledge through communication.

By contrast, Luhmann treats the evolution of social systems probabilistically, highlighting the contingent and highly improbable conditions of social reality. While in the Weberian model individuals exist within a social system as a unified entity, Luhmann's conceptual framework presents a desubjectivized perspective, de-emphasizing the role of the social actor as the primary motivational and intentional centre of social action. Rather, it is individual actions that shape one's involvement in specific social systems.

Luhmann's system theory departs from Parsons's postulation. While Parsons tends to deem system as having steady properties because it is founded upon mutual consensus, Luhmann sees it differently. He thinks that the nature of system is relatively unstable, owing to the fact that a system is not built upon consensus, rather it is built by and upon social interaction. The concept of social interaction also covers the concepts of conflict and social change -something that Parsons had failed to recognise. The recognition of social interaction concept affirms that Luhmann's concept prioritises function more than it prioritises structure. 23 neer and Nassehi, as cited by Hardiman, identified three points of modification that Luhmann had made to Parsons's concept. The first modification is, that social systems are not founded upon norms structure or other certain structure that dominate the society, rather, it is founded upon social interaction. This thought finds its root from the complexity of problems (norms and other) in the society. Luhmann saw a system from its presence compared to other social systems. This point of view is distinct from Parsons's, who deemed that social system exists singularly for itself. 

The second modification is the attitude towards Parsons's theory, which says that a system will collapse if certain systemic functions are disturbed. Luhmann presented that social systems can replace the damaged functions with alternative functions, thereby assuring the system to keep operating. 24 e third modification relates with the maintenance and sustainability of social system. For Parsons, the highest social unit is social system, therefore there is nothing outside social system. Luhmann reached another formulation: that the highest social unit is the world (Welt), therefore the existence of a social system is relative if compared to the other social systems.

The pattern variables structure the interaction system by offering solutions to the dilemmas of social action (Parsons, 1966, p. 59-66). 

The social system, however, is not an empirically given, concrete reality, but only a theoretical model of it. A social system is a way of defining certain relations between the components of 'action' that specifically relate to this reality (Parsons, 1970, p. 839). In the concept of social system, the mutual interactions of individuals are comprised, but perceived from the side of the structure of this interdependence, i.e. certain 'emergent' properties to which the system as a whole is entitled, with the interrelated interactions as a foundation. From the point of view of the properties of the social system as a whole, the orientations and actions of individuals are expressed in terms of position and role, i.e. their place in the structure of social relations and normatively regulated behaviour. In this respect, Parsons states clearly that the position and role are not attributes of empirically given subjects of action, but primarily parts of the social system that should be theoretically expressed in this form. Hence, the social system does not include the individual subject of action, understood as a concrete system of action, but only a part of the latter, expressed in the concept of role. Yet, the role has the function of an element connecting the action system of the individual subject with the social system (Parsons, Shils, 1959, p. 190;Parsons, 1965, p. 42). However, from the point of view of the social system, a role is an element in the general pattern that determines the action of the individuals that make up the system. In other words, an essential aspect of the social structure is a system framed in patterns of expectations that determine the appropriate behaviour of individuals performing certain roles (Parsons, 1972, p. 307). 

The social interaction system as a whole has, according to Parsons, its own functional needs. He lists four basic needs: adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, latency or pattern maintenance (the so-called AGIL model). At the most general level of a social system, each function is fulfilled by a distinct sub-system, each of which also has a similar structure of functional needs.

Snippet: General systems theory was outlined in 1969 by Ludwig von Bertalanffy who researched the organization of complex systems and provides a set of logical assertions about causality in organizations. Von Bertalanffy (1969) believed a system to be a complex network of interacting elements that continuously interact with their environments. Through this interaction, they transform and thus continuously evolve. Von Bertalanffy (1969) also believed these systems course-correct based on feedback. Building upon general systems theory, social systems include patterns and networks of individuals from various origins or statuses that roll into groups or structures that carry out diverse functions.

Title: Social relations: Building on Ludwig von Bertalanffy
Snippet: Ludwig von Bertalanffy did not leave us a legacy of a social systems theory. Nonetheless, reconstructing his general approach to systems provides us with several ideas on how to build a theory of social systems. The concept of social relations easily connects to Bertalanffy's concept of relations of organization. His way of thinking underlines that social relations, as any relations of organization, are unobservables that long for theoretical means of understanding. His conception of the world would assign social relations a special place in a hierarchy of processes internal to a social system — they represent the whole of the sys-tem that nonetheless emerges from the interaction of the actors as parts thereof. Last but not least, his world view would orient us towards an organization of social systems in which the dialectic of social relations and actors balances unity and diversity as an Ought. These three main ideas of Bertalanffy offer system theoretical pillars that can inspire current social theory.

Title: On the history of Ludwig von Bertalanffy’s “General Systemology”, and on its relationship to cybernetics – part III: convergences and divergences
Snippet: Bertalanffy’s so-called “general system theory” (GST) and cybernetics were and are often confused: this calls for clarification. In this article, Bertalanffy’s conceptions and ideas are compared with those developed in cybernetics in order to investigate the differences and convergences. Bertalanffy was concerned with first order cybernetics. Nonetheless, his perspectivist epistemology is also relevant with regard to developments in second order cybernetics, and the latter is therefore also considered to some extent. W. Ross Ashby’s important role as mediator between GST and cybernetics is analysed. The respective basic epistemological approaches, scientific approaches and inherent world views are discussed. We underline the complementarity of cybernetic and “organismic” trends in systems research within the unitary hermeneutical framework of “general systemology”.
