Snippet: This study is anchored on the Systems Theory as propounded by Ludwig von Bertalanffy. Systems theory is the interdisciplinary study of systems in general, with the goal of elucidating principles that can be applied to all types of systems at all nesting levels in all fields of research. The term originates from Bertalanffy's General System Theory (GST) and is used in later efforts in other fields, such as the action theory of Talcott Parsons and the social systems theory of Niklas Luhmann. In this context the word systems is used to refer specifically to self-regulating systems, i.e. that are selfcorrecting through feedback. Self-regulating systems are found in nature, including the physiological systems of our body, in local and global ecosystems, and in climate-and in human learning processes (Von Bertalanffy, 1968). 

As a transdisciplinary, interdisciplinary and multiperspectival domain, the area brings together principles and concepts from ontology, philosophy of science, physics, computer science, biology, and engineering as well as geography, sociology, political science, psychotherapy (within family systems therapy) and economics among others. Systems theory thus serves as a bridge for interdisciplinary dialogue between autonomous areas of study as well as within the area of systems science itself. Systems theory became the name used by early investigators for the interdependence of relationships created in organizations by defining a new way of thinking about science and scientific paradigms. System in this frame of reference is composed of regularly interacting or interrelating groups of activities. 

The systems view is a world-view that is based on the discipline of System Inquiry. Central to systems inquiry is the concept of SYSTEM. In the most general sense, system means a configuration of parts connected and joined together by a web of relationships. The Primer group defines system as a family of relationships among the members acting as a whole. Von Bertalanffy (1968) defined system as "elements in standing relationship" (Von Bertalanffy, 1968). The systems view was based on several fundamental ideas. First, all phenomena can be viewed as a web of relationships among elements, or a system.

Snippet: Bertalanffy, (1972), a German scientist, introduced systems theory in the 1930s at a philosophy seminar at the University of Chicago. Initially developed in the context of life sciences, systems theory has evolved into the modern field of ecology. He defined a system as a coherent entity with discernible boundaries, distinguishing internal and external elements and identifying input and output relationships (Bertalanffy, 1972). Systems theory is a theoretical perspective that analyses phenomena as an interconnected wholes rather than as isolated components. Lai, (2017) believed that understanding a system required examining its interconnected components rather than isolating individual parts. In his work "General Systems Theory: Essays on Its Foundation and Development," by Bertalanffy outlines the objectives of systems theory as: (1) integration of various sciences, (2) development of a general theory of systems, (3) advancement of exact theory in non-physical fields, (4) establishment of unifying principles across different sciences, and (5) integration of scientific education (Bertalanffy, 1972). While systems theory was not originally intended for applications in communication, family studies, or applied science, it has proven valuable in understanding the systems of the world around us. Through systems theory, we can gain a deeper understanding of the world and explore problems and their underlying causes (Bertalanffy, 1972;Khuzwayo, 2020). 

Systems can be found in nature, science, society, economics, and information systems (Larsson et al., 2010). A distinctive characteristic of systems theories is their simultaneous development across various disciplines. Scholars working from a systems theory perspective often build upon knowledge and concepts developed within other fields. Examples included natural and ecological sciences, with concepts such as organic aspects, homeostasis, and equifinality. 

Additionally, systems theory can also be used to develop and evaluate effective environmental policies and interventions by considering the interconnectedness of different environmental factors (Leydesdorff, 1996). This view correlates with this study which examines the road safety environment. This includes safety strategies, mediating human, environmental, vehicle, and road infrastructure factors in a coherent manner to ensure the utmost safety of the road.

attempts.answer:
Below is a structured synthesis that (1) lays out widely used elements of social systems, and (2) evaluates whether decentralized blockchain governance protocols instantiate those elements. Where possible, we connect mechanisms (e.g., token voting, staking, slashing) to core social-function components and discuss empirical evidence on how well they work in practice.

1) What “social systems” are: core elements and properties
- Foundational elements. Across social systems theory, common elements include a structure (stable roles, institutions, interaction patterns), functions (activities that meet system and member needs), a normative structure (rules, laws, moral norms and values), mechanisms of self‑regulation (adaptation, regulation, transformation), and openness to exchange resources and information with the environment <cite id="52b9fb49-2">Structure, functions, normative structure, and mechanisms of self-regulation are recurrent features of social systems; openness to environment is emphasized as a defining characteristic</cite>. This aligns with Parsons’ AGIL framing—adaptation, goal attainment, integration/pattern maintenance, and latent function maintenance—as functional imperatives fulfilled by interacting subsystems <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Parsons defines society as a self-regulating system fulfilling adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, and pattern maintenance needs</cite><cite id="52b9fb49-2">Parsons’ AGIL model highlights functional balance among subsystems</cite>. In role-theoretic terms, roles and positions are elements through which individuals are integrated into the system; the social system is “a way of defining relations between components of action” oriented by norms and expectations <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles and positions are parts of the social system that connect individual action with the system; the system comprises pattern variables that structure interaction via norms and expectations</cite>.
- Sociotechnical layering. When technical artifacts are deeply involved, sociotechnical systems exhibit emergent properties, non‑determinism due to human operators, and multiple, sometimes conflicting objectives; governance must negotiate these trade‑offs across political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions <cite id="f2b4af88-1">Sociotechnical systems have emergent properties, are non-deterministic because behavior depends in part on human operators, and involve complex relationships with several objectives; the study spans sociotechnical transitions, social practice, and related theories</cite>. A broader systems perspective stresses components, connections, scale/context, and the need to jointly analyze components and their interactions to explain system behavior <cite id="f2b4af88-0">Components, connections, scale, and context are central to system analysis; combining components with connections is key to explaining system functioning</cite>.
- Summary test. A social system has: (i) agents integrated via roles; (ii) normative rules governing behavior; (iii) communicative interaction producing order and adaptation; (iv) feedback/learning mechanisms (adaptation, regulation, transformation); and (v) boundaries with an environment through which resources and information flow <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles, norms, and pattern variables structure interaction and system-level functions</cite><cite id="52b9fb49-2">Normative structure and mechanisms of self-regulation are core; openness to exchange with environment is characteristic</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Human-in-the-loop introduces non-determinism and multi-objective trade-offs</cite>.

2) Decentralized blockchain governance: mechanisms and observed practices
- Governance-by-contract. DAOs encode governance logic in smart contracts: token-holding stakeholders propose and vote on amendments; token weight determines influence; participation and eligibility are regulated by governance contract design (e.g., registration, staking, proxies) <cite id="345e1e36-0">A DAO empowers token holders to manage protocol via a governance contract that defines participation and influence; decentralization and autonomy are core tenets</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Governance contracts exhibit autonomy of governance (self-governance) and decentralization via referendum-style voting; only a small fraction of token holders often vote</cite>.
- Voting mechanisms and design space. DAOs use diverse schemes: relative-majority/approval, token-based quorums, quadratic voting, liquid/conviction/weight-based voting, rage quitting, and holographic consensus; each trades off decentralization, expressive power, and coordination efficiency <cite id="345e1e36-4">Voting mechanisms include Approved Relative Majority, Token-Based Quorum, Quadratic Voting, Liquid Democracy, Weighted Voting, Rage Quitting, Holographic Consensus; Conviction Voting adjusts weight over time; different schemes impact outcome legitimacy</cite>. Conceptual work emphasizes a “governance triangle” linking smart contracts, distributed ledgers, and voting mechanisms, and proposes multi-dimensional evaluation (e.g., SEED) to capture decentralization and performance <cite id="345e1e36-2">A DAO governance triangle clarifies relationships among smart contract, ledger, and voting; a five-tier decentralization scheme and SEED metrics guide voting design</cite>.
- Incentives, participation, and centralization. Empirical studies find that despite token-weighted voting, voting power is highly concentrated: in Compound and Uniswap, as few as 3–5 voters often control majorities; costs and frictions (time, tokens at stake) disproportionately burden small holders; strategic behaviors (delays, coalitions) skew outcomes <cite id="345e1e36-1">As few as 3–5 voters swayed most proposals; voting costs disproportionately burden small token holders; strategic behaviors distort outcomes</cite>. Across 48 Ethereum DAOs, mechanisms intended to improve security or participation (token registration, staking, delegation) systematically concentrate voting power, revealing trade‑offs among decentralization, security, and usability <cite id="345e1e36-0">Token registration, staking, and delegation contribute to concentration of voting power, revealing trade-offs between decentralization, security, and usability</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Only a small number of voters often control outcomes; causes include high cost of voting, small high-power voters, collusion, or apathy</cite>. Legal standing remains unsettled: jurisdictions like Wyoming and Cayman recognize DAO entities, yet there is no widely accepted formal legal definition of what a DAO is, complicating legitimacy and accountability mappings to traditional institutions <cite id="345e1e36-3">There is no widely accepted formal/legal definition of a DAO; however, some jurisdictions allow DAO registration as legal entities</cite>.
- Sustainability and metrics. Work on DAO longevity proposes integrated KPIs that combine on-chain participation, treasury, and proposal automation, noting that despite diverse mechanisms (e.g., approval, rank-based, conviction), power concentration persists and requires measurement via indices like Gini and Nakamoto coefficients <cite id="345e1e36-4">Voting power remains concentrated in most DAOs; comprehensive frameworks are needed; common measures include Gini and Nakamoto coefficients</cite>.

3) Do decentralized blockchain governance protocols satisfy the elements of social systems?
- Roles/agents and social structure. DAOs instantiate roles and status via token holdings and governance contract functions: stakeholders are positioned as proposers, voters, delegates, and enforcers; token weight creates asymmetric influence and a hierarchy of participation <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles are elements of the social system; pattern variables structure expectations and behavior</cite><cite id="345e1e36-0">Governance contracts define how stakeholders participate and how much influence they have; token holders manage the protocol</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Governance mechanisms regulate who can vote and how, shaping participation hierarchies</cite>. However, because roles are “framed in patterns of expectations” by the protocol code and token distribution, they are tightly coupled to technical design and initial allocation, which may distort egalitarian role access and interaction norms <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles are parts of the social system expressed in patterned expectations</cite><cite id="345e1e36-0">Influence is determined by token holdings; design choices affect power distribution</cite>.
- Normative structure and rules. On-chain constitutions and governance contracts codify explicit amendment rules, quorum/turnaround thresholds, and sanctioning clauses; these are formal norms that can be audited and executed automatically, offering transparency and rule consistency <cite id="345e1e36-0">Governance is explicitly encoded in the DAO’s governance contract, defining participation and influence</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Token-based quorums, approval voting, and related mechanisms shape outcome legitimacy</cite>. In practice, enforcement is often economic: staking/slashing withdraws voting or funds when rules are violated, and proxy/registration gates eligibility; these are codified sanctions that regulate behavior <cite id="345e1e36-3">Voter registration, staking, and proxy voting regulate which token holders can vote and how; mechanisms protect voting from interference while encouraging participation</cite>.
- Communication and interaction. Governance cycles (proposal → discussion → voting → enactment) create channels for deliberation and coordination among stakeholders, often mediated by on-chain events and social interfaces; yet empirical costs and strategic voting reduce inclusive deliberation, with participation concentrated among a few wallets <cite id="345e1e36-1">Empirical analysis of 370 proposals shows centralization of voting power, burdens on small holders, and strategic behaviors; despite decentralized ideals, current mechanisms fall short</cite>. The sociotechnical layer amplifies non‑determinism: human behavior under token incentives, time and coordination frictions, and network effects produce emergent outcomes that are not functions of inputs alone <cite id="f2b4af86-1">Sociotechnical systems exhibit emergent properties and non-determinism due to human operators</cite><cite id="345e1e36-1">Strategic and coalition behaviors distort outcomes</cite>.
- Feedback, learning, and adaptation. DAOs can update their own governance rules via self-referential amendment processes, embodying autonomy of governance and a loop from outcomes to rule revisions; nevertheless, repeated empirical centralization suggests weak feedback to the membership and limited redistribution of power <cite id="345e1e36-3">Governance tokens can amend governance contracts themselves, with decisions by referendum-style voting</cite><cite id="345e1e36-0">Design mechanisms (registration, staking, delegation) both improve security/participation and can reinforce centralization, revealing trade-offs</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Despite diverse mechanisms, voting power remains concentrated; integrated KPIs are proposed to capture sustainability</cite>. Sustainability analyses recommend multi-metric feedback loops that combine participation, treasury health, and automation to guide adaptation, acknowledging that present designs often lack these integrative controls <cite id="345e1e36-4">Comprehensive frameworks for DAO sustainability remain underdeveloped; KPI-based approaches are proposed</cite>.
- Openness and integration with environment. DAOs interact with external agents, markets, and institutions; they import token economies, DeFi smart contracts, and off-chain communities, and may be recognized or contested legally; this situates them as open systems coupled to broader socio‑technical environments <cite id="52b9fb49-2">Social systems are open, exchanging resources, information, and energy with environments</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Legal definitions are unsettled but some jurisdictions allow DAO registration; DAOs integrate with broader environments</cite>. In DeFi ecosystems, governance extends across protocols (e.g., lending, exchanges), with cross‑influence on liquidity, risk, and user trust—classic multi‑objective trade‑offs for sociotechnical systems <cite id="f2b4af88-1">Sociotechnical systems involve interactions with political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions and face multi-objective trade-offs</cite>.
- Legitimacy, authority, and accountability. Because authority derives from code and token distribution rather than hierarchical managerial recruitment, legitimacy rests on procedural fairness, stakeholder consent, and external legal recognition; evidence shows that concentration of voting power and strategic voting undermine perceived legitimacy and accountability, even when formal rules are transparent <cite id="345e1e36-3">DAO governance is distinguished from traditional organizations by self-governance via referenda and decentralization, yet participation is low and power is concentrated</cite><cite id="345e1e36-1">Centralization and burdens on small token holders suggest current DAO governance mechanisms fall short of equitable decision-making</cite>. Some progress has been made in formalizing DAOs as entities and in proposing governance evaluation frameworks, but an accepted definition and consistent mapping to institutional accountability remain lacking <cite id="345e1e36-3">Only a small number of voters control outcomes; jurisdictions allow registration; no widely accepted formal definition</cite><cite id="345e1e36-2">Conceptual frameworks (governance triangle, SEED) aim to evaluate decentralization and performance</cite>.

4) Practical mapping: elements satisfied vs. gaps
- Roles and status: Satisfied in practice via token-based stakeholder classes and governance functions; however, initial token distributions and staking/registration can skew roles toward a small minority <cite id="345e1e36-0">Token holdings determine influence; governance defines participation roles</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Registration, staking, and delegation shape who can participate and how</cite>.
- Norms and rules: Explicitly codified and auditable; amendment processes provide self‑rule; but empirical studies show rule outcomes can reflect concentration and strategy rather than broad consent <cite id="345e1e36-0">Rules are encoded in governance contracts</cite><cite id="345e1e36-1">Outcomes swayed by few voters and strategic behavior suggest governance shortfalls</cite>.
- Interaction and communication: Channels exist for proposal and vote; yet low participation, cost barriers, and coalition dynamics reduce deliberative equality and pluralistic integration <cite id="345e1e36-1">Few voters sway most proposals; small holders face higher costs; strategic behaviors distort outcomes</cite>.
- Self-regulation, sanctions, and adaptation: Staking/slashing and eligibility gates provide economic and procedural sanctions; yet persistent centralization and thin feedback to the whole membership limit adaptive self‑regulation and may necessitate complementary off‑chain processes <cite id="345e1e36-3">Voter registration, staking, and proxy mechanisms protect voting and encourage participation</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Voting power concentration persists; integrated KPIs are proposed to guide adaptation</cite>.
- Openness and integration: Strong coupling to external DeFi infrastructures and markets; legal recognition is emerging but inconsistent; this creates legitimacy risks when governance outcomes face external scrutiny or fail to align cross‑system objectives <cite id="345e1e36-3">No accepted legal definition; jurisdictions allow registration</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Interactions span political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions</cite>.
- System boundaries and emergence: Clear technical boundaries (code, treasury, token supply) shape behavior; emergent properties arise from incentive structures and network effects, producing non‑deterministic outcomes to similar inputs <cite id="52b9fb49-2">Social systems maintain boundaries with environment and are open</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Emergent properties and non-determinism stem from human-in-the-loop sociotechnical systems</cite>.

5) Evaluating “satisfaction”: criteria and current verdict
- If the criterion is formal instantiation of roles, codified norms, and feedback loops, many DAOs score well: they have explicit rules, token-weighted roles, and amendment processes with sanctions and participation gates <cite id="345e1e36-0">Governance is explicitly encoded; token-weighted influence</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Autonomy of governance via self-amendment; decentralization via referenda</cite>. 
- If the criterion is inclusive, legitimate, and accountable social ordering across all members, evidence shows persistent shortfalls: concentration of voting power, participation barriers, and strategic manipulation undermine procedural fairness and accountability, revealing tension between decentralization and effective coordination <cite id="345e1e36-1">As few as 3–5 voters sway outcomes; burdens and strategic behaviors distort governance</cite><cite id="345e1e36-0">Design mechanisms can reinforce centralization despite intent to improve participation/security</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Voting power remains concentrated across many DAOs; integrated KPIs are needed</cite>. 
- If the criterion is sociotechnical coherence and multi-level governance, DAOs demonstrate emergent, non‑deterministic dynamics and cross‑system objectives (security, usability, decentralization), but often lack integrated feedback across participation, treasury, and proposal automation that would qualify as robust self‑regulation at the system level <cite id="f2b4af88-1">Sociotechnical systems exhibit emergent and non-deterministic behavior and multi-objective trade-offs</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Comprehensive sustainability frameworks remain underdeveloped</cite>.

6) What would make blockchain governance “satisfy” social-system elements more fully
- Strengthen role equity: reduce participation barriers (lower-cost voting, asynchronous deliberation), prevent collusion and sybil capture via identity-aware participation calibrated by incentive alignment and governance budgets <cite id="345e1e36-1">Voting costs disproportionately burden small token holders; strategic behaviors and coalition formation distort outcomes</cite>. 
- Enhance legitimacy via feedback: integrate multi-metric KPIs (participation, conviction, outcome quality, treasury, automation) into amendment voting and rotating supermajority requirements that penalize lopsided majorities without broad consensus <cite id="345e1e36-4">Integrated KPI-based approaches are proposed; concentration persists; measures like Gini/Nakamoto capture inequality</cite>. 
- Clarify accountability and external interfaces: adopt accepted legal forms and reporting standards; create bridges to off-chain community assemblies and audits; align with environmental governance norms to manage cross‑system objectives and risks <cite id="345e1e36-3">Lack of widely accepted legal definition complicates legitimacy; some jurisdictions recognize DAOs</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Governance must negotiate interactions across political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions</cite>. 
- Improve communication and deliberation: embed structured deliberation layers (e.g., proposal scoring, evidence repositories, liquid democracy with reputation) and use expressive voting schemes (conviction/quadratic) to better aggregate intensity and uncertainty <cite id="345e1e36-2">Evaluation frameworks (SEED) and governance triangle aim to capture decentralization and performance</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Conviction and approval voting affect outcome legitimacy; diverse mechanisms exist but need better integration</cite>.

Conclusion
- Elements of social systems. Widely supported elements include a stable structure of roles and institutions; a normative structure of rules and values; functions for adaptation, goal attainment, integration, and pattern maintenance; mechanisms of self‑regulation via communication, sanctions, and feedback; and openness to the environment <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles and norms structure interaction and system-level functions</cite><cite id="52b9fb49-2">Structure, functions, normative structure, self-regulation, and openness characterize social systems</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Sociotechnical systems exhibit emergent, non-deterministic behavior and multi-objective trade-offs</cite>.
- Do decentralized protocols satisfy them? They satisfy several core elements strongly—explicit rules, token-based roles/status, sanctionable behavior, self-referential amendment, and open coupling to markets and institutions. But they often fail to instantiate inclusive communication and broad legitimacy due to concentrated voting power, participation costs, and strategic manipulation, revealing persistent trade‑offs between decentralization and effective, accountable governance <cite id="345e1e36-0">Governance-by-contract encodes roles/weights and enables self-amendment</cite><cite id="345e1e36-1">Empirical centralization and strategic behaviors indicate shortfalls despite decentralized ideals</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Concentration persists; comprehensive sustainability frameworks are needed</cite>. In short, decentralized blockchain governance “does a good job” on codified norms and formal roles, but still struggles with communicative inclusion and institutional legitimacy relative to mature social systems; progress will likely come from integrated feedback metrics, deliberation layers, and clearer legal-institutional anchoring <cite id="345e1e36-2">Conceptual evaluation frameworks highlight decentralization and performance dimensions</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">DAOs’ self-governance and decentralization are distinct from traditional organizations, yet participation is low and power is concentrated</cite>.

Title: Frontiers in socio-environmental research : components, connections, scale, and context
Snippet: The first core feature across scholarship in this arena is the premise of a social-environmental (or social-ecological or human-natural) distinction. Although there have been some challenges to this distinction from the humanities and HEF, it remains an organizing principle for SE research, reflecting the disciplinary communities and types of knowledge that SE scholarship seeks to unite. Given the shared commitment to this distinction, it is the responsibility of the SE community to give due consideration to both parts of the system. Although in any particular application of these frameworks, the social and ecological elements of the system may not be equally important or wellunderstood, responsible practice requires that analysts consider social and ecological contributions at least as potentially of equal importance. 

The second core feature is that components, connections, scale, and context play central roles in SE systems. These four categories emerge as important to SE system analysis when the six frameworks are considered in aggregate: components as the building blocks that constitute an SE system; the type, directionality, and characteristics of the connections linking components; the ways in which different frameworks grapple with scale, scale mismatch, and cross-scalar interactions; and the different conceptualizations of the contexts surrounding SE systems. Despite significant variation in the relative emphasis and https://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol23/iss3/art23/ elaboration of different foundational elements across SE frameworks, these four foundational elements emerge as central to SE system conceptualization. 

The third shared principle relates to the practice of SE research. 

In particular, trade-offs emerge as a key feature of SE scholarship. Despite the differences among the compared frameworks, each of the frameworks provides effective points of entry in terms of understanding the complexity of SE systems. Our analysis highlights that there are many ways a system can be reduced; however, frameworks that succeed at conceptualizing components do a relatively poor job considering connections and vice versa. Finding a way to combine components and connections, to understand both what the critical components of a system are and how they interact, would strengthen theory of how and why SE systems function as they do and potentially lead to solutions for the complex problems they seek to understand. Likewise, theoretical development and empirical data seem to be inversely related in SE research.
</snippet>

Title: An Examination of the Complexity of the Large Sociotechnical Space System
Snippet: More than other complex systems, the design and development of social systems should be amenable to insights and heuristics. Social factors, after all, are notoriously difficult to measure, much less predict. However, like heuristics, they are associated with experience, failures as well as successes, and lessons learned [49] (p. 105). 

A sociotechnical system is defined as a system that incorporates technical components, operational processes, and individuals who utilize and interact with the technical system as part of a social system. Sociotechnical systems possess three key characteristics. Firstly, they exhibit emergent properties of the system of a whole that depend on the system components and their relationships. Secondly, they are non-deterministic, meaning they do not always produce the same output when presented with the same input, because the system's behavior is partially dependent on human operators. Thirdly, complex relationships with several objectives do not just depend on the system itself [55]. 

The study of sociotechnical changes has a long-standing tradition involving a wide array of methods that seek to address the complex interaction between social and technical realms. A thorough investigation undertaken by Sovacool and Hess revealed a plethora of theoretical and conceptual frameworks, encompassing a minimum of 22 distinct academic domains. A total of 14 theories were identified in the study as being of particular significance to at least 10% of the consulted experts. These theories include sociotechnical transitions, social practice theory, discourse theory, domestication theory, and large technical systems [56]. 

In this theoretical framework, the concept of large sociotechnical systems (LTSs) was introduced by Hughes [57,58] and subsequently developed by other experts in the field [59][60][61]. The objective of this development was to study and analyze how complex technologies interact with the political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions. In essence, an LTS can be defined as a "complex" system, comprising a substantial (if indeed countable) number of elements whose interactions are non-linear and thus whose nature is not merely the summation of its individual components.
</snippet>

Title: Social Systems Theory as Theoretical Framework for Human Resource Management ? Benediction or Curse? Introduction to the Special Issue
Snippet: Social systems theory as developed by Luhmann (Luhmann 1984) and used in organisation theory (see, e.g., Kasper et al. 1998;Hernes/Bakken 2003) and HR (see, e.g., Wolfgang Mayrhofer: Social Systems Theory as Theoretical Framework for HRM Mayrhofer 1996) is one of the theory candidates HRM can use to better understand itself and, at the same time, contribute to better practice. Beyond doubt it is one of the grand social theories of the past 30 years. Like comparable efforts (see, e.g., Giddens 1984;Bourdieu 1977) it provides a unified framework for the analysis of social reality at a highly aggregated level. 

In terms of theory history, there is no unified social systems theory as there is no singly systems theory, too. There seems to be consensus that systems are units differentiated from the environment and consist of at least two interrelated and distinguishable elements. Beyond that, a number of different theoretical traditions have developed systems theoretical views that are partly compatible with each other and partly are principally different from each other.
</snippet>

Title: Improving theories of change in conservation projects
Snippet: Conceptually, there are numerous similarities among the different theory of change approaches, as multiple authors have noted (e.g., Mayne, 2015;Rogers, 2014;Stein & Valters, 2012). To identify common components within the existing theory of change frameworks, we conducted a literature search via the Web of Science, Google, and Google Scholar of English-language theory of change approaches/ frameworks/guides that provided specific steps/components/elements for creating a theory of change and that were published between January 2012 and December 2023. We also reviewed the references in the included guides to identify other theory of change documents. 

We then conducted a structured analysis of the guides to identify the components for developing a theory of change with a high level of agreement. We chose a guide with a comprehensive list of components as our starting point (Noble, 2019). Two people then independently double-extracted the components from each guide and reached a consensus on the common components. Where there was 70% or greater agreement among the guides on a specific component of a theory of change, we included it in our approach. Our thinking was that each new approach drew on the existing theory of change thinking, and the included components represent the authors' views of what is important, and thus the consensus components of a theory of change reflect the more important components of a theory of change. 

After identifying the common components of a theory of change, we ordered the components in a logical sequence and developed written guidance for each component. Title: Émile Durkheim and Talcott Parsons: sociological ideas
Snippet: This paper explores the foundational sociological contributions of Émile Durkheim and Talcott Parsons, two central figures in the development of structural functionalism. Durkheim emphasized the role of social facts, collective conscience, and social solidarity in maintaining social order, arguing that society exists beyond the individual and shapes human behavior through shared norms and values. His work on anomie and the division of labor laid the groundwork for understanding the complexities of modern social structures. Building on Durkheim’s legacy, Parsons developed a more systematic theory of social systems, focusing on the interdependence of societal components through his AGIL schema. He conceptualized society as a self-regulating system that fulfills key functional imperatives to maintain stability. While both theorists underscore the importance of social cohesion and value consensus, Parsons introduced a more abstract and generalized model of societal functioning. Together, their work provides critical insight into how societies maintain order, manage change, and integrate individual actions within broader institutional frameworks.
</snippet>

Title: Disputes over the concept of social system and the critique of sociological reason
Snippet: The pattern variables structure the interaction system by offering solutions to the dilemmas of social action (Parsons, 1966, p. 59-66). 

The social system, however, is not an empirically given, concrete reality, but only a theoretical model of it. A social system is a way of defining certain relations between the components of 'action' that specifically relate to this reality (Parsons, 1970, p. 839). In the concept of social system, the mutual interactions of individuals are comprised, but perceived from the side of the structure of this interdependence, i.e. certain 'emergent' properties to which the system as a whole is entitled, with the interrelated interactions as a foundation. From the point of view of the properties of the social system as a whole, the orientations and actions of individuals are expressed in terms of position and role, i.e. their place in the structure of social relations and normatively regulated behaviour. In this respect, Parsons states clearly that the position and role are not attributes of empirically given subjects of action, but primarily parts of the social system that should be theoretically expressed in this form. Hence, the social system does not include the individual subject of action, understood as a concrete system of action, but only a part of the latter, expressed in the concept of role. Yet, the role has the function of an element connecting the action system of the individual subject with the social system (Parsons, Shils, 1959, p. 190;Parsons, 1965, p. 42). However, from the point of view of the social system, a role is an element in the general pattern that determines the action of the individuals that make up the system. In other words, an essential aspect of the social structure is a system framed in patterns of expectations that determine the appropriate behaviour of individuals performing certain roles (Parsons, 1972, p. 307). 

The social interaction system as a whole has, according to Parsons, its own functional needs. He lists four basic needs: adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, latency or pattern maintenance (the so-called AGIL model). At the most general level of a social system, each function is fulfilled by a distinct sub-system, each of which also has a similar structure of functional needs.
</snippet>

Title: Dysfunctions and Transformational Processes in Social Systems under Contemporary Global Changes
Snippet: Among these, the economic, political, legal, cultural, and social subsystems are most commonly distinguished. Each of them performs specific functions while remaining closely connected with the others and influencing their functioning. This interdependence between subsystems determines both the stability and the vulnerability of social systems in the face of internal and external challenges. 

Every social system is characterized by certain structural and functional features that determine the way it operates and develops. These include: − Structurea relatively stable pattern of social roles, institutions, and interactions between them; 

− Functionsactivities and processes aimed at satisfying the fundamental needs of society and its members; 

− Normative structurea system of rules, laws, moral norms, and values that regulate the behavior of individuals and groups; 

− Mechanisms of self-regulationprocesses of adaptation, regulation, and transformation that enable the system to respond to internal tensions and external influences. 

The development of the systems approach in the social sciences is closely associated with the theoretical contributions of a number of scholars. A particularly significant contribution in this field is the structuralfunctional theory of the American sociologist Talcott Parsons. According to his concept, society represents a system of interacting subsystems that must fulfill certain functional requirements in order to ensure the stability and sustainability of the social order. Parsons formulated four fundamental functions that every social system must perform: adaptation, goal attainment, integration, and latency (pattern maintenance). This model, known as the AGIL framework, emphasizes the necessity of maintaining functional balance among the different elements of the social system. 

Further development of social systems theory can be observed in the works of the German sociologist Niklas Luhmann, who proposed a different interpretation of social reality. According to his theory, society can be understood as a system of communications rather than merely a collection of individuals or institutions. Social systems, according to Luhmann, reproduce themselves through continuous communication processes that create and maintain the boundary between the system and its environment. This perspective directs attention to the role of information, communication, and interpretation in processes of social interaction. 

Despite the differences between various theoretical approaches, most scholars agree that social systems possess a number of common characteristics that define their nature and mode of functioning. Among the most important characteristics are: 

− Opennesssocial systems actively interact with their external environment and exchange resources, information, and energy;

Because of the lack of clarity, or maybe because the definition of social structure points to different aspects of the social structure, scientists often avoid defining social structure in their papers, and thereby contribute to the general confusion. Title: On the Centralization of Governance Power in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations
Snippet: A decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) is a governing entity that empowers its stakeholders (i.e., users who hold one or more of its tokens) to manage blockchain-based protocols (i.e., smart contracts) collaboratively. The governance of a DAO is explicitly encoded in the DAO’s governance contract, which defines how stakeholders participate in governance and how much influence (or voting power) they have in any decision. While decentralization and autonomy are the fundamental tenets of a DAO’s design, empirical evidence suggests that in practice governance is often highly centralized. In this work, we study the designs and implementations of 48 public and actively used DAOs, with substantially large capital, deployed on Ethereum. We identify how three key governance mechanismstoken registration, staking, and delegation-originally introduced to improve security or participation, contribute to the concentration of voting power. Unlike prior work on centralization of voting power in specific DAOs, our findings reveal that these governance mechanisms of DAOs themselves systematically reinforce centralization. By elucidating the relationship between governance design and voting centralization, this work advances the understanding of DAO governance structures and highlights the inherent trade-offs between decentralization, security, and usability of DAOs.
</snippet>

Title: Understanding Blockchain Governance: Analyzing Decentralized Voting to Amend DeFi Smart Contracts
Snippet: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) have emerged as a novel governance mechanism in blockchain ecosystems, particularly within Decentralized Finance (DeFi). By enabling token holders to propose and vote on protocol changes, these systems promise transparent and equitable decision-making without centralized control. In this paper, we present an in-depth empirical study of the governance protocols of Compound and Uniswap, two of the most widely used DAOs in DeFi. Analyzing over 370 governance proposals and millions of on-chain events from their inception until August 2024, we uncover significant centralization of voting power: as few as 3--5 voters were sufficient to sway the majority of proposals. We also find that the cost of voting disproportionately burdens smaller token holders, and that strategic voting behaviors, such as delayed participation and coalition formation, further distort governance outcomes. Our findings suggest that despite their decentralized ideals, current DAO governance mechanisms fall short in practice.
</snippet>

Title: Insight Into Voting in DAOs: Conceptual Analysis and a Proposal for Evaluation Framework
Snippet: As a new type of Internet-native organization in Web 3 relying on blockchain technology, DAOs are promising tools to organize user networks in Web 3. As the prominent decisionmaking method in DAO governance, voting needs to be carefully designed. This paper analyses the serious role of voting in DAOs and proposes a DAO governance triangle which clarifies the relationship between the smart contract, the distributed ledger and the voting mechanisms in DAO governance. To follow the most important feature, decentralization in DAO voting, a five-tier decentralization scheme is proposed to identify the decentralization demands in DAO voting comprehensively. To design a well-performing DAO voting, the evaluation metrics scheme of DAO voting, named SEED, is proposed in multiple dimensions to conceptually guide the design of DAO voting mechanisms. This paper is an opening remark on the conceptual analysis and the evaluation framework of the DAO voting. The specific voting entities' design and optimization need to be quantified and modelled in future work.

Title: On the Centralization of Governance Power in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations
Snippet: While recent legislation in a few places, e.g., Wyoming, Vermont and Cayman Islands, allow a DAO to be registered as a legal entity [6]- [8], there exists no widely accepted formal or legal definition for what constitutes a DAO. Yet, governance contracts underlying DAOs share two characteristic features: (i) autonomy of governance, or self-governance, whereby the current governance token holders have the power to amend the governance contract themselves and (ii) decentralization of governance, whereby all decisions, are arrived at through a referendum-style vote by all governance token holders. This decentralized decision making crucially distinguishes DAOs from traditional organizations, which recruit managers and entrust them with making such decisions. Decentralized Governance in Practice Recent studies [9]- [11] have shown that in many DAOs only a small number (and fraction) of all governance token holders participate in voting on governance proposals. Messias et al. [9] found, for instance, that in Compound, on average, as few as 3 voters controlled the majority of exercised votes and, hence, control the outcome of a proposal. Similarly, Fritsch et al. [10] observed that in most DAOs, just three voting wallets held more than 50% of exercised voting power. Low stakeholder participation risks concentrating the decision making in hands of a few, undermining the ideals of decentralized governance. 

Prior work have speculated about the causes of this centralization-attributing it to factors such as the high cost of voting, a small number of voters with high voting power, voter collusion, or voter apathy. Much less attention has been paid, however, to the effects of mechanisms adopted by DAOs to protect the governance voting from undue interference and malicious attacks, while encouraging eligible voter participation. In this work, we focus on three widely used mechanisms namely, voter registration, token staking, and proxy voting that allow DAOs to regulate which of their token holders can exercise their right to vote and how.
</snippet>

Below is a structured synthesis that (1) lays out widely used elements of social systems, and (2) evaluates whether decentralized blockchain governance protocols instantiate those elements. Where possible, we connect mechanisms (e.g., token voting, staking, slashing) to core social-function components and discuss empirical evidence on how well they work in practice.

1) What “social systems” are: core elements and properties
- Foundational elements. Across social systems theory, common elements include a structure (stable roles, institutions, interaction patterns), functions (activities that meet system and member needs), a normative structure (rules, laws, moral norms and values), mechanisms of self‑regulation (adaptation, regulation, transformation), and openness to exchange resources and information with the environment <cite id="52b9fb49-2">Structure, functions, normative structure, and mechanisms of self-regulation are recurrent features of social systems; openness to environment is emphasized as a defining characteristic</cite>. This aligns with Parsons’ AGIL framing—adaptation, goal attainment, integration/pattern maintenance, and latent function maintenance—as functional imperatives fulfilled by interacting subsystems <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Parsons defines society as a self-regulating system fulfilling adaptation, goal-attainment, integration, and pattern maintenance needs</cite><cite id="52b9fb49-2">Parsons’ AGIL model highlights functional balance among subsystems</cite>. In role-theoretic terms, roles and positions are elements through which individuals are integrated into the system; the social system is “a way of defining relations between components of action” oriented by norms and expectations <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles and positions are parts of the social system that connect individual action with the system; the system comprises pattern variables that structure interaction via norms and expectations</cite>.
- Sociotechnical layering. When technical artifacts are deeply involved, sociotechnical systems exhibit emergent properties, non‑determinism due to human operators, and multiple, sometimes conflicting objectives; governance must negotiate these trade‑offs across political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions <cite id="f2b4af88-1">Sociotechnical systems have emergent properties, are non-deterministic because behavior depends in part on human operators, and involve complex relationships with several objectives; the study spans sociotechnical transitions, social practice, and related theories</cite>. A broader systems perspective stresses components, connections, scale/context, and the need to jointly analyze components and their interactions to explain system behavior <cite id="f2b4af88-0">Components, connections, scale, and context are central to system analysis; combining components with connections is key to explaining system functioning</cite>.
- Summary test. A social system has: (i) agents integrated via roles; (ii) normative rules governing behavior; (iii) communicative interaction producing order and adaptation; (iv) feedback/learning mechanisms (adaptation, regulation, transformation); and (v) boundaries with an environment through which resources and information flow <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles, norms, and pattern variables structure interaction and system-level functions</cite><cite id="52b9fb49-2">Normative structure and mechanisms of self-regulation are core; openness to exchange with environment is characteristic</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Human-in-the-loop introduces non-determinism and multi-objective trade-offs</cite>.

2) Decentralized blockchain governance: mechanisms and observed practices
- Governance-by-contract. DAOs encode governance logic in smart contracts: token-holding stakeholders propose and vote on amendments; token weight determines influence; participation and eligibility are regulated by governance contract design (e.g., registration, staking, proxies) <cite id="345e1e36-0">A DAO empowers token holders to manage protocol via a governance contract that defines participation and influence; decentralization and autonomy are core tenets</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Governance contracts exhibit autonomy of governance (self-governance) and decentralization via referendum-style voting; only a small fraction of token holders often vote</cite>.
- Voting mechanisms and design space. DAOs use diverse schemes: relative-majority/approval, token-based quorums, quadratic voting, liquid/conviction/weight-based voting, rage quitting, and holographic consensus; each trades off decentralization, expressive power, and coordination efficiency <cite id="345e1e36-4">Voting mechanisms include Approved Relative Majority, Token-Based Quorum, Quadratic Voting, Liquid Democracy, Weighted Voting, Rage Quitting, Holographic Consensus; Conviction Voting adjusts weight over time; different schemes impact outcome legitimacy</cite>. Conceptual work emphasizes a “governance triangle” linking smart contracts, distributed ledgers, and voting mechanisms, and proposes multi-dimensional evaluation (e.g., SEED) to capture decentralization and performance <cite id="345e1e36-2">A DAO governance triangle clarifies relationships among smart contract, ledger, and voting; a five-tier decentralization scheme and SEED metrics guide voting design</cite>.
- Incentives, participation, and centralization. Empirical studies find that despite token-weighted voting, voting power is highly concentrated: in Compound and Uniswap, as few as 3–5 voters often control majorities; costs and frictions (time, tokens at stake) disproportionately burden small holders; strategic behaviors (delays, coalitions) skew outcomes <cite id="345e1e36-1">As few as 3–5 voters swayed most proposals; voting costs disproportionately burden small token holders; strategic behaviors distort outcomes</cite>. Across 48 Ethereum DAOs, mechanisms intended to improve security or participation (token registration, staking, delegation) systematically concentrate voting power, revealing trade‑offs among decentralization, security, and usability <cite id="345e1e36-0">Token registration, staking, and delegation contribute to concentration of voting power, revealing trade-offs between decentralization, security, and usability</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Only a small number of voters often control outcomes; causes include high cost of voting, small high-power voters, collusion, or apathy</cite>. Legal standing remains unsettled: jurisdictions like Wyoming and Cayman recognize DAO entities, yet there is no widely accepted formal legal definition of what a DAO is, complicating legitimacy and accountability mappings to traditional institutions <cite id="345e1e36-3">There is no widely accepted formal/legal definition of a DAO; however, some jurisdictions allow DAO registration as legal entities</cite>.
- Sustainability and metrics. Work on DAO longevity proposes integrated KPIs that combine on-chain participation, treasury, and proposal automation, noting that despite diverse mechanisms (e.g., approval, rank-based, conviction), power concentration persists and requires measurement via indices like Gini and Nakamoto coefficients <cite id="345e1e36-4">Voting power remains concentrated in most DAOs; comprehensive frameworks are needed; common measures include Gini and Nakamoto coefficients</cite>.

3) Do decentralized blockchain governance protocols satisfy the elements of social systems?
- Roles/agents and social structure. DAOs instantiate roles and status via token holdings and governance contract functions: stakeholders are positioned as proposers, voters, delegates, and enforcers; token weight creates asymmetric influence and a hierarchy of participation <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles are elements of the social system; pattern variables structure expectations and behavior</cite><cite id="345e1e36-0">Governance contracts define how stakeholders participate and how much influence they have; token holders manage the protocol</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Governance mechanisms regulate who can vote and how, shaping participation hierarchies</cite>. However, because roles are “framed in patterns of expectations” by the protocol code and token distribution, they are tightly coupled to technical design and initial allocation, which may distort egalitarian role access and interaction norms <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles are parts of the social system expressed in patterned expectations</cite><cite id="345e1e36-0">Influence is determined by token holdings; design choices affect power distribution</cite>.

- Communication and interaction. Governance cycles (proposal → discussion → voting → enactment) create channels for deliberation and coordination among stakeholders, often mediated by on-chain events and social interfaces; yet empirical costs and strategic voting reduce inclusive deliberation, with participation concentrated among a few wallets <cite id="345e1e36-1">Empirical analysis of 370 proposals shows centralization of voting power, burdens on small holders, and strategic behaviors; despite decentralized ideals, current mechanisms fall short</cite>. The sociotechnical layer amplifies non‑determinism: human behavior under token incentives, time and coordination frictions, and network effects produce emergent outcomes that are not functions of inputs alone <cite id="f2b4af86-1">Sociotechnical systems exhibit emergent properties and non-determinism due to human operators</cite><cite id="345e1e36-1">Strategic and coalition behaviors distort outcomes</cite>.
- Feedback, learning, and adaptation. DAOs can update their own governance rules via self-referential amendment processes, embodying autonomy of governance and a loop from outcomes to rule revisions; nevertheless, repeated empirical centralization suggests weak feedback to the membership and limited redistribution of power <cite id="345e1e36-3">Governance tokens can amend governance contracts themselves, with decisions by referendum-style voting</cite><cite id="345e1e36-0">Design mechanisms (registration, staking, delegation) both improve security/participation and can reinforce centralization, revealing trade-offs</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Despite diverse mechanisms, voting power remains concentrated; integrated KPIs are proposed to capture sustainability</cite>. Sustainability analyses recommend multi-metric feedback loops that combine participation, treasury health, and automation to guide adaptation, acknowledging that present designs often lack these integrative controls <cite id="345e1e36-4">Comprehensive frameworks for DAO sustainability remain underdeveloped; KPI-based approaches are proposed</cite>.
- Openness and integration with environment. DAOs interact with external agents, markets, and institutions; they import token economies, DeFi smart contracts, and off-chain communities, and may be recognized or contested legally; this situates them as open systems coupled to broader socio‑technical environments <cite id="52b9fb49-2">Social systems are open, exchanging resources, information, and energy with environments</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Legal definitions are unsettled but some jurisdictions allow DAO registration; DAOs integrate with broader environments</cite>. In DeFi ecosystems, governance extends across protocols (e.g., lending, exchanges), with cross‑influence on liquidity, risk, and user trust—classic multi‑objective trade‑offs for sociotechnical systems <cite id="f2b4af88-1">Sociotechnical systems involve interactions with political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions and face multi-objective trade-offs</cite>.
- Legitimacy, authority, and accountability. Because authority derives from code and token distribution rather than hierarchical managerial recruitment, legitimacy rests on procedural fairness, stakeholder consent, and external legal recognition; evidence shows that concentration of voting power and strategic voting undermine perceived legitimacy and accountability, even when formal rules are transparent <cite id="345e1e36-3">DAO governance is distinguished from traditional organizations by self-governance via referenda and decentralization, yet participation is low and power is concentrated</cite><cite id="345e1e36-1">Centralization and burdens on small token holders suggest current DAO governance mechanisms fall short of equitable decision-making</cite>. Some progress has been made in formalizing DAOs as entities and in proposing governance evaluation frameworks, but an accepted definition and consistent mapping to institutional accountability remain lacking <cite id="345e1e36-3">Only a small number of voters control outcomes; jurisdictions allow registration; no widely accepted formal definition</cite><cite id="345e1e36-2">Conceptual frameworks (governance triangle, SEED) aim to evaluate decentralization and performance</cite>.

4) Practical mapping: elements satisfied vs. gaps
- Roles and status: Satisfied in practice via token-based stakeholder classes and governance functions; however, initial token distributions and staking/registration can skew roles toward a small minority <cite id="345e1e36-0">Token holdings determine influence; governance defines participation roles</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Registration, staking, and delegation shape who can participate and how</cite>.
- Norms and rules: Explicitly codified and auditable; amendment processes provide self‑rule; but empirical studies show rule outcomes can reflect concentration and strategy rather than broad consent <cite id="345e1e36-0">Rules are encoded in governance contracts</cite><cite id="345e1e36-1">Outcomes swayed by few voters and strategic behavior suggest governance shortfalls</cite>.
- Interaction and communication: Channels exist for proposal and vote; yet low participation, cost barriers, and coalition dynamics reduce deliberative equality and pluralistic integration <cite id="345e1e36-1">Few voters sway most proposals; small holders face higher costs; strategic behaviors distort outcomes</cite>.
- Self-regulation, sanctions, and adaptation: Staking/slashing and eligibility gates provide economic and procedural sanctions; yet persistent centralization and thin feedback to the whole membership limit adaptive self‑regulation and may necessitate complementary off‑chain processes <cite id="345e1e36-3">Voter registration, staking, and proxy mechanisms protect voting and encourage participation</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Voting power concentration persists; integrated KPIs are proposed to guide adaptation</cite>.
- Openness and integration: Strong coupling to external DeFi infrastructures and markets; legal recognition is emerging but inconsistent; this creates legitimacy risks when governance outcomes face external scrutiny or fail to align cross‑system objectives <cite id="345e1e36-3">No accepted legal definition; jurisdictions allow registration</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Interactions span political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions</cite>.
- System boundaries and emergence: Clear technical boundaries (code, treasury, token supply) shape behavior; emergent properties arise from incentive structures and network effects, producing non‑deterministic outcomes to similar inputs <cite id="52b9fb49-2">Social systems maintain boundaries with environment and are open</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Emergent properties and non-determinism stem from human-in-the-loop sociotechnical systems</cite>.

5) Evaluating “satisfaction”: criteria and current verdict
- If the criterion is formal instantiation of roles, codified norms, and feedback loops, many DAOs score well: they have explicit rules, token-weighted roles, and amendment processes with sanctions and participation gates <cite id="345e1e36-0">Governance is explicitly encoded; token-weighted influence</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">Autonomy of governance via self-amendment; decentralization via referenda</cite>. 
- If the criterion is inclusive, legitimate, and accountable social ordering across all members, evidence shows persistent shortfalls: concentration of voting power, participation barriers, and strategic manipulation undermine procedural fairness and accountability, revealing tension between decentralization and effective coordination <cite id="345e1e36-1">As few as 3–5 voters sway outcomes; burdens and strategic behaviors distort governance</cite><cite id="345e1e36-0">Design mechanisms can reinforce centralization despite intent to improve participation/security</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Voting power remains concentrated across many DAOs; integrated KPIs are needed</cite>. 
- If the criterion is sociotechnical coherence and multi-level governance, DAOs demonstrate emergent, non‑deterministic dynamics and cross‑system objectives (security, usability, decentralization), but often lack integrated feedback across participation, treasury, and proposal automation that would qualify as robust self‑regulation at the system level <cite id="f2b4af88-1">Sociotechnical systems exhibit emergent and non-deterministic behavior and multi-objective trade-offs</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Comprehensive sustainability frameworks remain underdeveloped</cite>.

6) What would make blockchain governance “satisfy” social-system elements more fully
- Strengthen role equity: reduce participation barriers (lower-cost voting, asynchronous deliberation), prevent collusion and sybil capture via identity-aware participation calibrated by incentive alignment and governance budgets <cite id="345e1e36-1">Voting costs disproportionately burden small token holders; strategic behaviors and coalition formation distort outcomes</cite>. 
- Enhance legitimacy via feedback: integrate multi-metric KPIs (participation, conviction, outcome quality, treasury, automation) into amendment voting and rotating supermajority requirements that penalize lopsided majorities without broad consensus <cite id="345e1e36-4">Integrated KPI-based approaches are proposed; concentration persists; measures like Gini/Nakamoto capture inequality</cite>. 
- Clarify accountability and external interfaces: adopt accepted legal forms and reporting standards; create bridges to off-chain community assemblies and audits; align with environmental governance norms to manage cross‑system objectives and risks <cite id="345e1e36-3">Lack of widely accepted legal definition complicates legitimacy; some jurisdictions recognize DAOs</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Governance must negotiate interactions across political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions</cite>. 
- Improve communication and deliberation: embed structured deliberation layers (e.g., proposal scoring, evidence repositories, liquid democracy with reputation) and use expressive voting schemes (conviction/quadratic) to better aggregate intensity and uncertainty <cite id="345e1e36-2">Evaluation frameworks (SEED) and governance triangle aim to capture decentralization and performance</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Conviction and approval voting affect outcome legitimacy; diverse mechanisms exist but need better integration</cite>.

Conclusion
- Elements of social systems. Widely supported elements include a stable structure of roles and institutions; a normative structure of rules and values; functions for adaptation, goal attainment, integration, and pattern maintenance; mechanisms of self‑regulation via communication, sanctions, and feedback; and openness to the environment <cite id="52b9fb49-1">Roles and norms structure interaction and system-level functions</cite><cite id="52b9fb49-2">Structure, functions, normative structure, self-regulation, and openness characterize social systems</cite><cite id="f2b4af88-1">Sociotechnical systems exhibit emergent, non-deterministic behavior and multi-objective trade-offs</cite>.
- Do decentralized protocols satisfy them? They satisfy several core elements strongly—explicit rules, token-based roles/status, sanctionable behavior, self-referential amendment, and open coupling to markets and institutions. But they often fail to instantiate inclusive communication and broad legitimacy due to concentrated voting power, participation costs, and strategic manipulation, revealing persistent trade‑offs between decentralization and effective, accountable governance <cite id="345e1e36-0">Governance-by-contract encodes roles/weights and enables self-amendment</cite><cite id="345e1e36-1">Empirical centralization and strategic behaviors indicate shortfalls despite decentralized ideals</cite><cite id="345e1e36-4">Concentration persists; comprehensive sustainability frameworks are needed</cite>. In short, decentralized blockchain governance “does a good job” on codified norms and formal roles, but still struggles with communicative inclusion and institutional legitimacy relative to mature social systems; progress will likely come from integrated feedback metrics, deliberation layers, and clearer legal-institutional anchoring <cite id="345e1e36-2">Conceptual evaluation frameworks highlight decentralization and performance dimensions</cite><cite id="345e1e36-3">DAOs’ self-governance and decentralization are distinct from traditional organizations, yet participation is low and power is concentrated</cite>. </answer>

Title: Frontiers in socio-environmental research : components, connections, scale, and context
Snippet: The first core feature across scholarship in this arena is the premise of a social-environmental (or social-ecological or human-natural) distinction. Although there have been some challenges to this distinction from the humanities and HEF, it remains an organizing principle for SE research, reflecting the disciplinary communities and types of knowledge that SE scholarship seeks to unite. Given the shared commitment to this distinction, it is the responsibility of the SE community to give due consideration to both parts of the system. Although in any particular application of these frameworks, the social and ecological elements of the system may not be equally important or wellunderstood, responsible practice requires that analysts consider social and ecological contributions at least as potentially of equal importance. 

The second core feature is that components, connections, scale, and context play central roles in SE systems. These four categories emerge as important to SE system analysis when the six frameworks are considered in aggregate: components as the building blocks that constitute an SE system; the type, directionality, and characteristics of the connections linking components; the ways in which different frameworks grapple with scale, scale mismatch, and cross-scalar interactions; and the different conceptualizations of the contexts surrounding SE systems. Despite significant variation in the relative emphasis and https://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol23/iss3/art23/ elaboration of different foundational elements across SE frameworks, these four foundational elements emerge as central to SE system conceptualization. 

The third shared principle relates to the practice of SE research. 

In particular, trade-offs emerge as a key feature of SE scholarship. Despite the differences among the compared frameworks, each of the frameworks provides effective points of entry in terms of understanding the complexity of SE systems. Our analysis highlights that there are many ways a system can be reduced; however, frameworks that succeed at conceptualizing components do a relatively poor job considering connections and vice versa. Finding a way to combine components and connections, to understand both what the critical components of a system are and how they interact, would strengthen theory of how and why SE systems function as they do and potentially lead to solutions for the complex problems they seek to understand. Likewise, theoretical development and empirical data seem to be inversely related in SE research.

Title: An Examination of the Complexity of the Large Sociotechnical Space System
Snippet: More than other complex systems, the design and development of social systems should be amenable to insights and heuristics. Social factors, after all, are notoriously difficult to measure, much less predict. However, like heuristics, they are associated with experience, failures as well as successes, and lessons learned [49] (p. 105). 

A sociotechnical system is defined as a system that incorporates technical components, operational processes, and individuals who utilize and interact with the technical system as part of a social system. Sociotechnical systems possess three key characteristics. Firstly, they exhibit emergent properties of the system of a whole that depend on the system components and their relationships. Secondly, they are non-deterministic, meaning they do not always produce the same output when presented with the same input, because the system's behavior is partially dependent on human operators. Thirdly, complex relationships with several objectives do not just depend on the system itself [55]. 

The study of sociotechnical changes has a long-standing tradition involving a wide array of methods that seek to address the complex interaction between social and technical realms. A thorough investigation undertaken by Sovacool and Hess revealed a plethora of theoretical and conceptual frameworks, encompassing a minimum of 22 distinct academic domains. A total of 14 theories were identified in the study as being of particular significance to at least 10% of the consulted experts. These theories include sociotechnical transitions, social practice theory, discourse theory, domestication theory, and large technical systems [56]. 

In this theoretical framework, the concept of large sociotechnical systems (LTSs) was introduced by Hughes [57,58] and subsequently developed by other experts in the field [59][60][61]. The objective of this development was to study and analyze how complex technologies interact with the political, economic, institutional, and social dimensions. In essence, an LTS can be defined as a "complex" system, comprising a substantial (if indeed countable) number of elements whose interactions are non-linear and thus whose nature is not merely the summation of its individual components.

Title: Social Systems Theory as Theoretical Framework for Human Resource Management ? Benediction or Curse? Introduction to the Special Issue
Snippet: Social systems theory as developed by Luhmann (Luhmann 1984) and used in organisation theory (see, e.g., Kasper et al. 1998;Hernes/Bakken 2003) and HR (see, e.g., Wolfgang Mayrhofer: Social Systems Theory as Theoretical Framework for HRM Mayrhofer 1996) is one of the theory candidates HRM can use to better understand itself and, at the same time, contribute to better practice. Beyond doubt it is one of the grand social theories of the past 30 years. Like comparable efforts (see, e.g., Giddens 1984;Bourdieu 1977) it provides a unified framework for the analysis of social reality at a highly aggregated level. 

In terms of theory history, there is no unified social systems theory as there is no singly systems theory, too. There seems to be consensus that systems are units differentiated from the environment and consist of at least two interrelated and distinguishable elements. Beyond that, a number of different theoretical traditions have developed systems theoretical views that are partly compatible with each other and partly are principally different from each other.

Title: Improving theories of change in conservation projects
Snippet: Conceptually, there are numerous similarities among the different theory of change approaches, as multiple authors have noted (e.g., Mayne, 2015;Rogers, 2014;Stein & Valters, 2012). To identify common components within the existing theory of change frameworks, we conducted a literature search via the Web of Science, Google, and Google Scholar of English-language theory of change approaches/ frameworks/guides that provided specific steps/components/elements for creating a theory of change and that were published between January 2012 and December 2023. We also reviewed the references in the included guides to identify other theory of change documents. 

We then conducted a structured analysis of the guides to identify the components for developing a theory of change with a high level of agreement. We chose a guide with a comprehensive list of components as our starting point (Noble, 2019). Two people then independently double-extracted the components from each guide and reached a consensus on the common components. Where there was 70% or greater agreement among the guides on a specific component of a theory of change, we included it in our approach. Our thinking was that each new approach drew on the existing theory of change thinking, and the included components represent the authors' views of what is important, and thus the consensus components of a theory of change reflect the more important components of a theory of change. 

After identifying the common components of a theory of change, we ordered the components in a logical sequence and developed written guidance for each component. We then tested and refined the guidance. After each round of testing, we examined what happened, why it happened, and how to improve the process the next time (Morrison & Meliza, 1999). The learning objectives were to reduce pain points for project teams and increase the utility of the guidance. 

While there is widespread agreement on the specific components of a theory of change, the terminology for the various components of a theory of change remains heterogeneous. For example, activities, actions, strategies, strategic approaches, and interventions have all been used to describe the same component in a theory of change. We define our terms below and follow the Conservation Standards wherever possible (Table 1).
